speechtext:
Chapter 10, section 39 of the Revised Statutes of Canada 1906, reads as follows:
To the member occupying- the recognized position of leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons, there shall he payable an additional sessional allowance of $7,000.
The amendment which I propose will read as follows:	.
Section 39 of the Senate and House of Commons Act, Revised Statutes, 1906, chapter 10, is amended by striking out the words " additional sessional " in the third line thereof and

substituting therefor the words " additional annual."
When the Act was originally passed I do not think it was the intention that the allowance to the leader of the Opposition should be a sessional allowance, considering the fact that the Prime Minister of Canada is receiving an annual allowance of $10,000 per year, together with his sessional indemnity, and members of the Government are receiving $7,000 together with their sessional indemnities. In the event of two sessions, the Prime Minister receives $15,000 a year while the recognized leader of the Opposition receives $19,000 a year. I think that would indicate that it was the intention of Parliament in passing the Act that the allowance of the leader of the Opposition should be annual the same as that of the members of the Government. That is my explanation.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.

On the Orders of the Day:
Mr. E, GUSS PORTER (West Hastings): Mr. Speaker, before proceeding with the Orders of the Day, I desire to make a personal explanation in regard to a statement made by the hon. member for Chambly-Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) a day or two ago in the House in discussing the Grand Trunk Acquisition Bill. That statement found its way into the Ottawa Evening Citizen in its issue of the 4th inst. The statement in question is reported1 in that paper, as follows:
Mr. Archambault declared that in one in stance the whole Canadian National railways schedule had been interfered with for political purposes. He read letters [DOT] and newspaper articles dealing with the case of R. H. Thompson, of Mont Eagle Valley, Ont., who declared that because the C. N. R. train had been cancelled at Bancroft for the purpose of carrying people to E. Gus Porter's picnic at Marmora, his daughter whom he was taking to hospital at Toronto had died.
Neither the Citizen nor the hon. member for Chambly-Vercheres can be accused of originality in regard to this statement as it first appeared in a notorious publication known as Jack Canuck. So long as the report remained with such a disreputable publication as that, or in the hands of the hon. member for Ch.ambly-Vercheres, I did not consider the matter was such as to call for an explanation from myself. Both the statement and the inference from it seemed to be too silly to require any contradiction.
But the matter having found its way into Hansard and also into the respectable public press, I feel that in justice to myself, and to the Government managing the railway in question, I should make an explanation. It is said, as I have read, that the whole Canadian National railway schedule has been interfered with for the purpose of helping to make a success of my political picnic. I had no idea that I had acquired any such prominent position, as alleged, that I could have control of the whole Canadian National Railway system in order that I might hold it up and use it for the purposes of my picnic. However, that seems to be the allegation and the statement is just as devoid of truth as the conclusion is lacking in common sense. The facts are that on the day in question I did not have a single thing to do with the regulation or operation of the trains on this branch of railway in any manner, shape or form; nor did the committee in charge of the picnic which was held in my honour at that time. I have made inquiry and I have ascertained the fact to be that not a single train upon that railway altered its regular schedule time on that occasion. The trains ran regularly all day long and no application was made to the railway company to have them alter or change their schedule in that respect.
Hon. gentlemen may not know that on the Central Ontario branch of the Canadian National railway the station at Marmora, where this picnic was held, was about two miles distant from the village itself and that for the accommodation of the traffic at the village a branch line has been put in between the main line and the village. On the day in question the last train of the day operating to the south ran into the village and out again, as a pure matter of business and not as a result of any interference by myself or the committee, to pick up the hundreds of passengers living south of the village and to convey them to their homes.
The result was that the train was about one hour and a half late, not more than that.; and to convince hon. members that it was not due to any concerted action on the part of myself or the committee, the train left Marmora just as soon as the people could get on board. The train had been advertised to leave at six o'clock, but as a matter of fact it left some twenty or twenty-five minutes before that hour, and did not even wait for the picnic to break up. As regards the death of Mr. Thompson's daughter, I regret that exceedingly, as I am sure every one will, but my regret is still greater in that any hon. gentleman in

this House should make use of an incident of that kind to, as it appears to me, try and make some political capital. The hon. gentleman concludes his reference to this matter with the following language:

speechtext: On the motion of Sir George E. Foster, Bill No. 43, respecting a certain convention between His Majesty and the President of the French Republic, dated the 19th day of .September, 1907, and the convention supplementary thereto, and the French Convention Act, 1908, was read a second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Steele in the Chair.
This Bill has not been distributed and I want to see a copy of it before giving my assent to the measure.

The Bill has been distributed in French and English. The measure really explains itself but in a word this is what it means: The Treaty heretofore existing between France and ourselves was subject to determination on a year's notice to be given by either party. The French Government gave the year's notice which would have terminated the Treaty in September, 1919. They gave that notice-in pursuance of -a general policy intended to clear the decks for re-arrangements after the war was over-to all nations with whom the French had treaty agreements. There was nothing in these notifications which denoted a spirit of opposition either to existing agreements or to fresh treaties that might be contemplated-this course was adopted, as I have said, in pursuance of a general policy. Then in order not to have the Treaty lapse while matters were in a confused and unsettled condition, the French Government proposed that instead of a year's notice the Treaty should continue with a notice period of three months, and it is that substitution-having for its object the continuance of the existing agreement until conditions are such that further
CMr. Porter.]
negotiations may take place with reference to our commercial relations-that is provided for in the Bill.

I think the only regrettable feature of the matter is that the three months' notice seems exceedingly short. I can quite understand however, as was mentioned in the discussion on the resolution last night, that this is merely following the general policy of the French Government; it is not aimed at Canada particularly.
Not at all.

It is to be regretted that the three months' notice is so short because, as my right hon. friend knows, you can do very little in governmental affairs in that period. However, it is the general policy of the French Government and there is no use our objecting to it.

A short period like three months does interfere with the carrying out of trade on any projected plan. At the same time, as regards France and Canada during the present confused period, there is not very much trade being done in either direction.
The present arrangement is better than having the Treaty terminated.

Yes, and as my hon. friend has said, it is the proposition of the French Government itself.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

speechtext:
Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Minister of the Interior) moved that the amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 33, respecting the acquisition by His Majesty of the Grand Trunk Railway system, be read a second time and concurred in. He said: The first amendment made by the Senate is to clause 6, which provides for the arbitration of the value of the preference and common stocks. In line 13, of that clause after the word " Canada " the following addition has been made:
The value, If any, so determined shall not be greater than an amount on which the annual dividend at four per cent per annum on the aggregate face value of the present guaranteed stock and the new guaranteed stock taken together would exceed $5,000,000. The fixing of this limit shall not be taken by the arbitrators

as any admission or indication that the value to be determined is the amount so fixed, or any other amount.
The intended effect of the amendment, as hon. gentlemen will see, is to fix a maximum annual dividend of $5,000,000 to cover both the present guaranteed stock and the preference and common stock; that is to say, $2,500,000 is to cover the dividend that can be payable in respect of the award on the preference and common stock, the guaranteed stock representing the other $2,500,000. How the $5,000,000 is arrived at I do not know. But at all events it has pleased the Senate to fix a maximum of $2,500,000 as the utmost annual dividend that can be given in respect of the award to be made on the preference and common stock. I still hold the view expressed while this Bill was before the House that it is certainly unwise to place a maximum, for the reason I then expressed, namely, that it does intimate a feeling at all events that there might be the value stated in the maximum; and for the further reason that in connection with this arbitration the other parties to it in another country cannot be directly negotiated with in this connection, and are liable, I would think, to regard a maximum fixed by the one side as taking away from the arbitration the very essence of arbitration itself. For those reasons I think that it would be preferable not to fix a maximum. In this regard it differs from the Canadian Northern arbitration, inasmuch as in that case the holders of the stocks were here to negotiate with directly, they were our own citizens to the extent of over five-sixths of the whole stock; but the holders of these Grand Trunk stocks are overseas and are in no way subject to our jurisdiction, and we cannot come in personal and direct contact with them to reach any understanding or arrangement. However, from another standpoint, it is a safeguard, I suppose, to the extent that the maximum is fixed here, and the amendment is not of such a nature that we would feel justified in opposing it.
I would point out, however, that I do not think the clause is aptly phrased. It says that the award shall-not be greater than an amount on which the dividends would exceed $5,000,000 on the aggregate preference and common stocks. I think the word " equal " would be better than the word " exceed." But I have no doubt at all that the Board of Arbitrators will have no difficulty in determining what is the real intention of Parliament in this regard.
The second amendment merely substitutes the word " stock " for the word " stocks "
in line forty-six of clause 10. That is the preferable word, and I presume the plural form was a misprint in the original.
The third amendment is to insert after clause 11 the following as clause 12, a new clause:	.
For the purpose of the valuation provided in this Act, the obligations of the Grand Trunk as guarantors of any indebtedness of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company or of the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company or otherwise and the claims of the Government of the Dominion of Canada against either of the above-mentioned companies or against any company forming part of the Grand Trunk Railway system shall not be treated as extinguished or affected by anything contained in this Act.
If I were asked my personal opinion it would be that this clause is superfluous. I am quite unable to understand the apprehension of the Senate that the Chief Justice of the Exchequer Court might unless specially directed, value the stock irrespective of the obligation of the company whose stock it is; but I can see no injury to the Bill by the insertion of the clause, and consequently there is no reason why we should insist 'that it be removed.
I beg to move that the amendments made by the Senate in Bill No. 33, an Act respecting the acquisition by His Majesty of the Grand Trunk Railway system, be agreed to.

Mr. Speaker, with regard to the question of limitation, I agree very heartily with the argument of my hon. friend, but I am obliged to dissent from his conclusion, for after arguing one thing he did the very opposite. I quite concur in his view that it is a dangerous thing to put on this limitation at all, for it is open to the objection that it seems to be an invitation to the arbitrators to award that sum. The Senate appears to have anticipated that objection, and they have added some words to the effect that the arbitrators must not consider it as an admission of anything. But while they have done that, the fact remains that, the mere mention of that limitation is an intimation to the wide world that the arbitrators may award that sum, and no one will be very much surprised if they do award it. I regret that my hon. friend did not follow up his views by moving that this House should not concur in the amendment. I think if he had done so he would have found the House heartily in sympathy with him.
It strikes me that the form of the amendment is strange. It seems as if some one was exceedingly anxious to avoid the men-

tion of a big round sum. What the amendment means is that $2,500,000 will be required for the interest on the guaranteed stock, and the other $2,500,000 is to represent the balance as a maximum. That other $2,500,000 simply means another $60,000,000. Why the Senate do not state plainly that the award shall not exceed $60,000,000 I do not understand, unless some one thought that the mention of that sum might alarm the people, and that it might be camouflaged by merely mentioning the interest on that sum. It is a strange form of amendment to accomplish that which on examination is found, to be its purpose. However, that is a matter of no great consequence. If they wanted to say that the arbitrators should not award more than $60,000,000, why did they not say so in plain English? I am really unable to see what good end is served by concealing the fact that it means an invitation to the arbitrators, subject to the words, it is fair to say, that the Senate iput in, to award $60,000,000 to stocks which many people think are not worth any great sum at all.
I notice there appears to be some difficulty on the part of the Government in regard to this matter. Air. Speaker, I have not had anything to say with respect to this purchase of the Grand Trunk. I have always had the greatest respect for the Senate, but of all the absurd things I have ever seen in legislation, this business of appointing arbitrators to determine the value of a thing and then setting the price that they are to determine upon is the worst. Why should we appoint arbitrators to determine the value of anything, even if the thing to be valued is only a cow, and then set the price is more than I can comprehend. It is the most absurd thing I ever heard of, even if it was moved by the Senate.
Mr. FRANK S. CAHILL (Pontiac):	I
should like to hear the explanation of the minister in charge of this Bill as to why he wants this amendment to be adopted. He seemed to be quite definite a few days ago in the view' that there should be no changes in the Bill as presented, and no amendments. If one more vicious clause was required in the Bill, it has now been put in by the Senate. This stock that is to be arbitrated, if it is worth anything-which I very much doubt-was quoted in the London stock exchange at about $28,000,000 or $29,000,000. Why the members of the Government should invite the arbitrators to place a value of $60,000,000 on that stock is surely beyond the reasoning power of any man in this House, especially when we remember that it is the money of the people that is being voted away. Why, the Government in this Chamber were bad, but the Government out of this Chamber were forty times worse. It is a most ridiculous thing to set a limit of $62,000,000 upon stocks that are to-day absolutely worthless. There is absolutely no question that if the Government would demand payment from the Grand Trunk people that stock would not be worth one dollar, and the stocks that they are guaranteeing the interest on would not be worth half of what they are guaranteeing. We were told yesterday that the country was bone dry and stone broke; the soldiers came to the Government for assistance, but they did not have a dollar to give them. We did not have a cent; we did not have a dollar; our poor poverty-striken country was not able to make an allowance of one dollar to the soldiers. And now thirteen hours afterwards, the Government comes down with another invitation to the London stockholders to insist on

getting at least $60,000,000 for absolutely worthless stock. If I am in order, I would move in amendment that the word " dollars " be struck out of the Bill and the word " cents " substituted therefor.

speechtext:
I have very
grave doubts whether the House should concur in this amendment, which fixes or invites a fixation of the award at a certain amount. I think it goes far too high. During the course of the debate it was held out to us and repeated over and over again that the arbitrators might find no value at all.
The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) and the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) said that they did not know what the amount of the award might be; in fact, it was suggested to members of the House that the arbitrators might find that there was no value at all, and that what we were undertaking, directly and indirectly, besides the result of the arbitration, might be ample and sufficient to pay for anything that we are getting. By concurring in this amendment we are inviting the arbitrators to decide that there shall be an award of $62,500,000, and it seems to me that whatever the arbitrators may do, we are not justified in saying that they are doing right if they bring in an award of that kind. Personally, I cannot be a party to concurring in the suggestion that the arbitrators would be justified and that we say that they would be justified in bringing an award involving such an immense amount of money. I do not know that recrimination is any good or that comparisons should be made; but I say to the Government and to hon. gentlemen opposite that if we reached the conclusion that we did yesterday by such a huge majority in this House, namely, that we had not a dollar to spend to gladden the hearts and comfort the homes of our returned soldiers, and refused simply on that account to do anything beyond what we are doing along those lines, it is an extraordinary thing that the next morning we should come to this House and say that as far as we are concerned we should give away for this railroad, which is certainly not a paying proposition, $62,500,000 in addition to the hundreds of millions of dollars which we are obliging ourselves to pay.

speechtext: Hon. A. K. MACLEAN (for the Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved the second reading of Bill No. 42 to amend the Canada Shipping Act (pilotage).

I have not seen a copy of this Bill which is now being distributed for the first time. I regard it as somewhat extraordinary that a Bill of such far-reaching importance to the commercial life of the country should be moved before copies of it have reached hon. members. The other night when the resolution was before the House I gave the minister clearly to understand that I at all events was opposed to it and considered it a highly important measure. The least courtesy I would expect from the minister, therefore, would be that the Bill would be placed within the reach of the members a few minutes before the second reading. The second reading now synchronizes with the distribution of the Bill, the contents of which I do not know, for I have not had time to study it. It was explained, when the resolution was moved, that this measure means that the safeguards surrounding the seamen of this country are in future to be placed in the hands of men who are "not shipmasters; and

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
We are not at
that Bill yet. My hon. friend's remarks may be apropos in a few minutes, but at present a different Bill is before the House.

I beg your pardon. However, I objected yesterday to the Pilotage Bill to some extent, although my objection was not as strong as it is in regard to the measure to which I refer, which has for its purpose the giving of a free hand in maritime matters to persons who are not shipmasters. The minister says that the Pilotage Bill is before us, but my remarks will stand in regard to the other

Bill when it comes up. I must apologize to the minister for being perhaps a trifle hasty in my remarks, but as I have explained, I was under the impression that it was the other Bill and not the Pilotage Bill that was before the House. The Pilotage Bill does not appear to me to be as serious as the other.

I confess considerable ignorance of the subject matter of this measure, and as it has to do with a considerable portion of the navigation of British Columbia I am particularly interested in it and would be glad of an explanation from the minister as to the purport of the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: The Bill is to enable Canadian registered shipping operating between the province of British Columbia and American ports as far south as San Francisco, and sailing as far north as Alaska, to be relieved of pilotage. We are *simply giving the shipping owned in British Columbia the same relief that years ago was given to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and later to Quebec and Ontario shipping. As a matter of fact the law has been evaded for many years in British Columbia, and the class of shipping to which this Bill refers has not paid any pilotage.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and the House went into committee on the Bill, Mr. Steele in the Chair.
On section 1-Exempted ships:

Would it not meet the minister's purpose if he struck out the words "or ports' in the ninth line so that the clause would read: "Ships registered in Canada employed in voyages between any port in the province of British Columbia, and the port of San Francisco, or any port of the United States of America on the Pacific," etc.? The intention is that it shall apply only to foreign trade, but as the clause reads it would imply interprovincial trade.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
I agree with the hon.
gentleman, and therefore move that the words, " or ports ", in the ninth line be struck out.

speakerposition: stagedirection

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
Will the minister explain
why vessels registered in Canada should be exempted from pilotage dues while the same privilege is not accorded to vessels registered in the United States? A vessel plying daily between Seattle and Vancouver and calling at Victoria, if registered in the United States, will be subject to pilotage dues, but will be exempt if registered in Canada. If it is proper to protect the lives of passengers on United States boats by providing pilotage, is there any reason why the same protection should not be afforded passengers on Canadian ships? The crew might be Canadians on both boats. The minister might clear that point uip.

On the Pacific Coast, as in other local waters, we have ferries making daily trips, and the captains of these boats are excellent and most expert navigators in local waters. They never use a pilot, but under present regulations they have to pay pilotage dues, and this Bill empowers the pilotage authorities to relieve these ships of dues. The masters of passenger boats are highly qualified men and are expert in the navigation of the waters in which they daily travel, so that my hon. friend need have no apprehension in that regard.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
Some of these boats are
owned in Seattle and registered in the United States and some are registered in Canada. Why the difference?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's question has reference to a matter ether than that which it is intended to be dealt with in this Bill. Under the law as it now stands, the department by regulation can determine what pilotage American shipping shall pay in British Columbia waters, and the Department of Justice has so advised it. If we desired to relieve American shipping altogether of pilotage we would require further legislation. The department, however, does not desire to do this, but under the statute they are empowered to reduce to a minimum the pilotage rates on American shipping, and it is their intention td do so. I am informed that this is satisfactory to American shipping.

Will the Minister or
the hon. member (Mr. Stevens) tell us something about the pilotage system on the Pacific coast? I suppose they have more than one body of pilots. Are they paid by fixed salary or do they get their income by collecting pilotage dues from the different ships?

Up to a year ago the
pilotage in British Columbia waters was under two or three pilotage commissions, and the pilots were paid out of the fees

collected from the ships, and not by any fixed salary. The former Minister of Marine, Mr. Hazen, appointed, a commission, and some eminent authorities on pilotage went t'o British Columbia and made careful investigation and recommended that some system of pilotage should be inaugurated such as existed on the St. Lawrence and has recently been put into operation at Halifax.
This Bill is really giving effect to that part of the recommendation and of this new system which has been put into operation during the past few months. Pilotage will now be placed on a salary basis. The desire is to reduce pilotage which I always considered excessive, as I think many others do. We anticipate that it will be a benefit to shipping as well as to the pilots themselves.

I remember the Bill that my hon. friend refers to very well. It was before this House at a late stage of the last session. I remember discussing it with the minister at the time. I am pretty sure that it does not provide for salaries for the pilots on the Pacific coast. It fixes pilotage salaries on the St. Lawrence, and I think it has something to do with pilotage on the Atlantic coast at ports such as St. John, Halifax and Sydney. But it has not yet gone into operation. I remember telling the minister that he would find a good deal of trouble because all pilots whose salaries were not fixed would be looking for their fixation. The hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) will find there is no provision made for fixing the salaries of pilots on the Pacific coast in so far as any legislation of this House isi concerned. For that reason, although I have no request from, the pilots on the Pacific coast, I would be very sorry to cut down the little income-or whatever it may be, big or little-that the pilots on the Pacific coast are receiving.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: It is the same way with the pilots on the Atlantic coast.

Any pilot on the Atlantic coast who lost his pilotage dues is provided by this Parliament with a fixed salary. Now we are taking away the pilotage dues on the Pacific coast and substituting nothing. We are stripping them of their incomes and giving them nothing to take their places. The hon. member (Mr. A. K. Maclean) shakes his head. If he says that he is not taking away their incomes and that he is substituting something, I will have nothing to say. We must have pilots. Some of the ships on the coast of British 
Columbia going to the United States may not require pilots, but there are ships coming into these harbours that will require pilots, and unless there is some sufficient provision made to encourage pilots to remain at that business there will be no pilots at all. I would like to be satisfied in the general interest of the country and of its shipping that sufficient provision is being made for pilots on the Pacific coast to keep them at this work. If their dues are being removed or taken away it seems that something else will have to be substituted to take their place, and I have not been satisfied on that point.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: The average pilot in the various pilotage districts of British Columbia receives |300 per month. I think they earn more than do pilots in other districts in Canada unless it be at Quebec and in the St. Lawrence district. In 1918, in the Victoria-Esquimalt pilotage district five pilots earned 315,131; in the Nanaimo district seven pilots earned $22,275, and in the Vancouver district nine pilots earned $27,360. The earnings in the several pilotage districts were more than sufficient to pay these pilots the remuneration which I have stated.
These were all pilotage dues?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
They were pilotage dues and did not include dues paid by the class of shipping which we are trying to relieve by this present Bill. Perhaps it is unfortunate but we must admit that this tax was evaded under some regulation, or pretended regulation, by virtue of which there was a remission of the pilotage dues paid by the class of shipping sought to be relieved by this Bill. In no other place in Canada do we seek to tax for pilotage dues shipping engaged in running between Canadian and American ports except in British Columbia. Ships running from Sydney to New York pay no pilotage dues. The same is true of ships running between Halifax or St. John and New York, between Quebec and New York and between Sydney and Newfoundland. If Canadian ships, they pay no pilotage dues. We simply want to apply that same rule to British Columbia. Supposing it did affect the pilots' earnings in British Columbia, I do not admit that that is a serious consideration. The important consideration is the interest of shipping. Some other means will be provided for remunerating the pilots if the pilotage dues do not provide a fund. I do not see why we need to concern ourselves so much

about the interests of the pilots, as they must be suitably remunerated in one way if not in another. There is a more important consideration, namely: What are the interests of the province of British Columbia and of shipping? We are instructed that it is very much in the interest of the mercantile business of this province that this legislation become effective. I think it is also in the interest of the development of shipping.

Whiat representations from the shipping interests has the minister received? Can he give any evidence or satisfactory proof to the House derived from recognized shipping interests that there are objections in British Columbia to paying the pilotage dues? I am not familiar with the developments in regard to pilotage which the minister appears to have found out so recently. I know that a small schooner leaving Sydney and going to Halifax has to pay pilotage dues. The minister may shake his head but I have been in negotiation, as the lawyer for a client, trying to get from the pilotage authorities of the port of Halifax, $9 paid in pilotage fees by the owner of a small schooner. I did not get the money back. They refused to give it back; they said it was the law and that the owner of this schooner bad to pay pilotage due's coming into Halifax harbour because he was in the same class as anybody else. My hon. friend seems to have discovered a new law by which a great percentage of the shipping on our coasts goes free. I think that if he will inquire he will find that boats carrying coal from Louisburg to the New England States pay pilotage coming into the harbour of Louisburg. I am not giving that as a certainty but I would like my hon. friend to inquire. If a recognized body of shipowners, or a shipping federation, on the Pacific coast represent to this Government that they should not pay pilotage dues it is a matter for serious and proper consideration. But we have not heard of any such request from them, and until we have such I think this very important class of men- the pilots-should have some consideration. My hon. friend seems to be willing to brush the pilot aside and give hi's attention altogether to the shipowner. They are both very necessary to the commerce of this country and they should both receive fair treatment.

stance, the assertion that I had made a promise that this Bill would not be introduced this session is not correct. The Government is not insisting that this legislation shall be passed this session. I am sure, if
my hon. friend had only given a moment's consideration to the Bill, he would not have made the remarks he did. I do not know of any reason why he should not be aware of what the Bill contains, notwithstanding that the first reading only took place yesterday. Every hon. gentleman knows that in the concluding days of the session certain business-usually not very important business-must be accelerated in some form or other and the House invariably assents to that course. Will my hon. friend tell me his reason for , waiting until the last days of the session before introducing this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I moved the resolution upon which this Bill is founded four or five days ago.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
That is sufficient notice to the House. In fact, the suggestion for the legislation came before me from the Department of Marine and Fisheries only a few days ago.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is to empower the Minister of Marine to permit ships to leave Canadian ports without certificated masters and mates and notwithstanding the provisions of the Merchant Shipping Act. If the Bill is acceptable to the House, I purpose to amend it by providing that it shall he restricted to sailing ships and shall be operative only for the next six months. During the war an Order in Council was passed under the War Measures Act empowering the Minister of Marine to permit vessels to depart from Canadian ports without certificated masters and mates, if it were shown to him that it was not possible to get certificated officers and that the men for whom the permits were required were competent. These permits were always issued upon the representation of the Collector of Customs at the ship's port. As hon. gentlemen are aware, the War Measures Act and all Orders in Council passed under it may very quickly become inoperative, and upon the proclamation of peace there is some doubt as to the validity of Orders in Council which were stipulated to be in force during the period of the war and six months thereafter. It is a fact that in Canada to-day it is impossible to get the required number of certificated masters and mates to command ships on transatlantic voyages, there being a great many more Canadian ships, particularly sailing ships, at present engaged in the transatlantic business than at any time during the last twenty-five years. Many men have coasting certificates which under the statute are not acceptable for transatlantic voyages; but those men are to all intents and purposes just as competent to take ships across the Atlantic as men who have ocean-going certificates. During the last three years quite a number of permits of this nature were issued; for instance, from Nova Scotia ports 111 permits; from New Brunswick ports 41; from British Columbia ports 6, and from Quebec ports 2.
In the United States, as I pointed out the other day, sailing ships up to 700 tons gross can depart from any American port to any other port in the world without certificated officers. In Great Britain any freight ship may engage in coast-wise business without a certificated officer. The difficulties of navigating a ship around the waters of the United Kingdom are infinitely greater than those involved in the taking of a ship from a Canadian port across the Atlantic. I think there is a great deal of fallacy in the idea that a ship cannot be commanded except by a certificated person. I have no doubt that some day we will have enough sense to allow the man who owns a ship other than a passenger ship to send her anywhere he chooses, provided he is satisfied that the officers in charge are competent men.
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is to enable the minister for the next six months to do what he has been doing during the last two years, namely, to permit ships to depart from Canadian ports without certificated officers. A great many wooden ships have been built in Canada during the war, and war conditions prevented many of our seafaring men taking



the examination for masters' and mates' certificates. Consequently we are confronted with the practical question of whether or not Canadian ships shall be refused departure from our ports if they are unable to procure certificated officers. If there is any substantial objection I shall withdraw the motion.

This Bill provides by paragraph (b):
Canadian registered vessels carrying passengers not exceeding one hundred registered tons, which ply exclusively within what the Minister of Marine and Fisheries may deem to be sheltered waters within the inland waters or on the sea coasts of Canada.
Therefore this Bill deals with vessels plying on the sea coast of Canada as well as within inland waters.
Referring to what my hon. friend said in answer to the hon. member from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) as to the interview that certain members had with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, he will remember that I, together with some of my colleagues and representatives from the Quebec and Montreal pilots, saw him while he was Acting Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and he agreed with us that the matter should be postponed.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Surely my hon. friend does not mean to say that I discussed with him or any one else this particular Bill? I remember the occasion he refers to, but we were then discussing a matter which had reference solely to Quebec pilotage.
So we were.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: This Bill does not refer to that matter.

We were discussing the question of Quebec and Montreal pilotage, together with the question of masters and mates, and at that time my hon. friend agreed to wait until the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) could personally consider the question. Later on we interviewed the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and as I stated last night on resolution No. 15 relating to Bill No. 48, it was agreed that so far as pilotage was concerned, nothing would be done until the session of 1920.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I deny that.

I am not suggesting that my hon. friend himself said -so; I am speaking of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries,
[Mr. A. K. Maclean.!

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I was not even present at that meeting.
If my hon. friend denies that, let us postpone this question until he has had an opportunity of seeing the Minister of Marine and Fisheries personally; he is in the city.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I certainly shall not agree to postpone this Bill upon the ground my hon. friend suggests.

Mr. Speaker, I consider that this measure is without doubt a dangerous one, because it will allow unscrupulous ship-owners to employ incompetent men in certain waters.
The lives of the public, even of the men manning the vessels, would thereby be in danger, especially at this time of year. The men manning the vessels will be compelled to work with incompetent -masters and mates. The certificate of master can be obtained at any time, with few exceptions. It is true that there are some conditions and circumstances under which a master's certificate cannot be obtained, but very seldom would that be the case.
As I understand it, this legislation will apply to vessels of 100 tons. Suppose you had fifteen or twenty of these small vessels coming up or going down the St. Lawrence river and they met one or more of the big liners at -Isle au Grues on the north side of Beaujeu Bank or at lower traverse, St. Rochs, where the channel is very narrow. If a number of these small vessels are manned by men who are incompetent the lives of passengers may be endangered. This Bill is a bad one unless it is amended to apply to vessels plying only in certain waters.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: What has that to do with this Bill?
It has a great deal to do with the Bill, because you want to put incompetent men on the vessels.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I do not want to do that at all.
The Bill provides expressly against incompetency.

This matter is being taken up at the last hour of the session. The Shipping Federation is very anxious to have this Bill passed. There is a controversy-I hope my hon. friend will not deny it-between the Shipping Federation and masters and mates and pilots-

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: This Bill did not originate with or emanate from the Shipping Federation or from the pilotage authorities of any district. As a matter of fact, it was largely suggested by myself owing to the conditions in the Maritime Provinces. The controversy in the Quebec pilotage district does not relate to this Bill. All questions about the Quebec pilotage district are trifling and unimportant so far as this Bill is concerned.

The Bill relates to Quebec pilots.
Mr. A. K. 'MACLEAN: Not three ships leaving the port of Quebec within the next six months would apply for a permit under this legislation. Indeed, there would not be one; I have said that during the last three years only two such permits were issued in respect of the port of Quebec. I should like to hear from the leader of the Opposition; if he thinks that this Bill should not go through I will drop it.
II certainly do think so, and I take all the responsibility that may be thrown upon me for doing so.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. E. SINCLAIR (Prince Edward Island):
speechtext:
No good reason has been given why this Bill should be withdrawn. Conditions are existing in the Maritime Provinces which require that power be given to the minister to make the law applicable in respect of some of' the inland waters. In Prince Edward Island some ferry boats have been held up because of inability to obtain certified masters, and shippers and passengers have been very much inconvenienced. These boats have been running for three years under the same men who are now in command. I think that the minister is justified in bringing down this Bill; no danger is involved to the lives of passengers, because it is provided that the minister shall satisfy himself that the person in command of a vessel shall be competent to handle the vessel in the waters that it plies in or may ply in in future. I urge the minister not to withdraw the Bill. I think it is a proper Bill, and tt am prepared to support it.
Mr. A*. K. MACLEAN: I quite agree that this is important legislation. I am not at all impressed with the arguments that have been laid against it. They are unfounded and unpractical and are made without any concern for the national interest. However, the House is to prorogue to-day or Monday. This is not a Government Bill or a measure which the ministry is pressing as such through the House; it is a matter which is
122i
entirely within my own discretion. But inasmuch as hon. gentlemen take the position that the Bill was introduced only yesterday, and inasmuch as objections, which are, perhaps, technical, but which nevertheless have some force, have been raised, I do not feel that I should press the Bill. I, therefore, wish to withdraw the motion for the second reading.
The minister takes the responsibility of saying that those who are opposing this Bill are absolutely void of a proper conception of the national interest.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
No, I said the
grounds taken were made without any concern for the national interest.

That statement is
absolutely unfounded and should never have been made. I hold in my hand the British Shipping Act of 1894, and the people of Great Britain and Ireland have been leaders and kings of shipping and kings of the seas for at least the last two hundred years, and "Britannia rules the waves", notwithstanding the hon. member for Halifax. Section 92 of the British Shipping Act, in dealing with ships that cross* the Atlantic, states:
Every British foreign-going ship and every British home-trade passenger ship, when going to sea from any place in the United Kingdom, and every foreign steamship carrying passengers between places in the United Kingdom, shall be provided with officers duly certificated under this Act.
Yet, when I ask that we comply with that Act, I am told by a minister of this Government that I am void of a proper conception of the national interest. It is a pity that my hon. friend was not in England for the last hundred years or so to tell the people there what fools they are to require certificated masters. This happens to have been the common and statutory law for the last thousand years or so, but the hon. member for Halifax says that it should be wiped off the slate and that it is nonsense and unfounded twaddle to be supporting such contentions. Let me tell my hon. friend and the House that when Confederation was formed in 1867, the only subject in the commercial life of this country over which we were not given complete jurisdiction was that of shipping, and that was withheld because of shipping being a world-wide commercial matter, the ocean being its home and common ground for every nation on earth. The Canadian Statute, the Merchant Shipping Act, is based upon the British Shipping

Act, and the latter is binding upon us, and our Act requires the same consideration and obligations as to masters. We must, in the case of any ship over 100 tons, burden or upwards, have a certificated master and a certificated mate. That is my ground; I am standing by the British law and the Canadian law, and it is only on the most serious ground that those laws should be departed from, notwithstanding the minister's statement to the contrary.
Motion for second reading withdrawn.
Mr. A. K. MACLEAN moved that the order be discharged.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty, Bill No. 41 to amend the Railway Act, 1919, was read the second time.
On the motion of Mr. Doherty that the House do go into commitee on the Bill:
Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must point out to the hon. member for Pontiac, who has proposed to submit an amendment, that under decisions which have been given in the House for some time since the revision of the rules a few years ago, this motion is not debatable. In the public interest, however, I have deemed it wise that an exhaustive examination of the authorities, not only here but in the Mother Country, should be made for the purpose of establishing a definite practice to be followed in this House, and I hope that at an early stage of next session we may have settled for all time a proper practice in this regard. In the meantime, while I do not think it wise that the motion should be debatable, I mention the circumstance so that any discussion we may have may not be construed as a precedent.

I would take it, Mr. Speaker, that the Government has not considered it desirable to submit this Bill to a special committee. The clause which it is proposed to strike out from the' Bill is one that was the subject of considerable debate in committee at the last session of parliament when the revision of the Railway Act was under consideration. I have not had time to look up the debate on the question because the Bill was introduced only last night. But my recollection is that the railway employees were very insistent on having this clause inserted in the Bill.

I am not speaking positively, but I think it was pointed out at that time that the railway employees made a very strong and persistent fight that the clause should be inserted in the Railway Act. They contended that if it were not inserted certain railways that were not under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission were in a position to use rolling stock that was not up to the standard sanctioned by the commission, and that these lines endangered the lives of the employees. The employees were used to a certain standard rolling stock and equipment in the railways that were under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission, and they said that when they went on a line that was not under the commission they might find the rolling stock different.
The equipment and requirements would be different. The equipment that they were used to might not be employed on these lines and it would be a great menace to their safety, because a change that they were not looking for might cause death or accident. I think the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Morphy) was on that committee, and he will recollect the insistent fight that the railway employees put up to have this clause inserted. If this clause is being amended at the instigation of the railway companies, I think the railway employees should be consulted before the amendment is made. If this clause is only being eliminated at the instigation of the electrically-operated lines it should be made to apply to the electric railways only. If that is not done I think the Government would be well advised to withdraw this legislation until the railway employees have had an opportunity of presenting their case to the Railway Committee, the Government, or whoever will be handling this proposed legislation. I beg to move:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
" this Bill be committed to the Railway Committee for consideration of clauses suggested by the Special Railway Committee."

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: In view of the announcement that I made a short time ago, I trust that any debate on this motion will be of a limited character.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I quite appreciate what the hon. member (Mr. Cahill) said about the interests of the railway employees in the particular species of case to which he has referred. I was not here last session, but I have read the minutes of the discussion in the committee. I think he is correct in his statement that this clause was
enacted to meet the representations of railway employees engaged upon what we now call the large railways under the legislative authority of the Dominion Parliament, that
it was highly desirable, where companies were operating roads under provincial authority, that those roads so operated should be brought under Dominion authority so that the same requirements might apply to them. The reason why it is now proposed to repeal this section is that it is thought-and experience has shown-that altogether too wide a provision was made when seeking to attain that particular end; a provision which applies to railways where those conditions did not prevail at all and where it is looked upon as objectionable-and I think the objections have force-that purely local railways, merely by reason of the fact that they may have Acquired, or may be operating or leasing, some portion of a road which was originally constructed under a Dominion charter, and therefore treated as a work for the general advantage of Canada, subject to the control of Parliament and not subject at all to local control, either provincial or other control under provincial authority, should be made subject to the provision of this section. It was thought highly undesirable that you should produce that result. For instance, a notable case that is brought up of the effect of this section is the case of the British Columbia Electric Company, which as I understand it, is a company running tramways in Vancouver and Victoria.
New Westminster.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am informed that they also have a tramway in Victoria.
Yes, that is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It would appear that
that company is operating under lease or other arrangement-that is immaterial-two small lines of railway, one of which was originally constructed by the Canadian Pacific and the other under a Dominion charter, one road being the Vancouver and Lulu Island railway and the other Vancouver, Fraser Valley and Southern railway. By reason of their so operating these roads, under this section, these tramways have been withdrawn from the control of the provincial authority, they have ceased to be subject to the jurisdiction of the public utilities commission of British Cblumbia and have been placed under control of this Parliament in so far as legislative action is concerned and under the control of the

Board of Railway Commissioners in so far as the fixing of their rates is concerned.
This condition of affairs has given rise to very strenuous objection on the part of the provincial authorities, likewise upon the part of the local authorities, and I might perhaps correctly say, if I can take the representations of the representatives of the people, upon the part of the people of the province. It has been forced upon our attention the exceedingly widespread effect of this section as it stands.
There is also another very serious consideration. I do not desire to absolutely commit myself upon this question, but our attention having been brought to it, we felt called upon to look into the matter and there does arise a very serious question whether it is, under the British North America Act, open to this Parliament, by general legislation of this kind describing a class of works, to make every particular work come within the description of that class of work for the general advantage of Canada without the slightest reference to whether as an actual matter of fact in each particular case it can at all reasonably be suggested that that particular work is a work for the general advantage of Canada. It has been suggested that it is extremely doubtful whether the power vested in this Parliament to make of a work otherwise purely local a work for the general advantage of Canada and subject in consequence to the control of this Parliament by declaring it to be a work for the general advantage of Canada, entitles this Parliament to declare that all works of a certain kind shall be works for the general advantage of Canada without knowledge of the conditions, and entirely without reference to the circumstances, of each particular work.
The condition of affairs to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cahill) has pointed, and for which there seems to me to be a very strong reason for seeking a remedy, can be properly and adequately dealt with by taking up the case where the condition which he has pointed out exists and by declaring each one of these local railways which are being operated by railway companies under the control of Parliament to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. That will subject, these roads to the provisions of a law applicable to railways which are under the legislative authority of this Parliament. The difficulty seems to result not from the fact that the condition which the hon. gentleman has pointed out calls for remedy, but from the fact that the remedy applied did not fit the particular case, or at all events did

not confine itself to fitting the particular case, but operated to bring under this Parliament a large class of works which, I think it may be safely said, was not in contemplation at all at the time. Now this condition of affairs which has brought all these railways, or tramways, of the class I have referred to under the control of Parliament, is one, I think, that calls for rectification, and there is some urgency in remedying the condition that results from the fact that these enterprises find themselves to-day either entirely withdrawn from provincial control, or at all events in a' condition of doubt as to what authority controls them. I think the remedy will be-
May I ask the minister whether this Bill will have the effect of withdrawing such a railway as the Quebec and Saguenay from the jurisdiction of the Railway Board?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Not the Quebec and Saguenay.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hope hon. members will understand that we are not in committee. The motion before the House is that I do leave the Chair for the House to go info Committee of the Whole. It has been moved in amendment by the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) that the Bill be referred to the Railway Committee. If the amendment prevails discussion at this stage is quite useless. If it does not prevail, and the motion itself is accepted, hon. gentlemen will then have full opportunity to discuss the merits of the Bill in committee.
Question.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is on the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to have the opportunity of saying a word on the subject before the House, if it is possible, because I think a solution is possible that will obviate the existing difficulty.
I would like to have an answer to my question.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member's question is one which should be put in committee. There is at present a motion before the Chair and hon. members may recall that I have pointed out in rulings heretofore given, that this motion is not debatable. I suggested that the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) should have

an opportunity to make an explanation in moving this motion, but I trust the House will agree with me that it would be unwise to have a general discussion of the Bill at this stage.

The minister did not finish his statement.
Amendment negatived, motion agreed to and the Mouse went into Committee, Mr. Nesbitt in the Chair.
On section 1-application of Act to certain classes of railways repealed.

I' desire to oppose the passing of this Bill for reasons which were partly set forth by the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill). I am of the opinion that the minister is putting forward legislation for the benefit of a couple of local companies and wiping from the statute a clause which was inserted, after a good deal of discussion, at the request of the men who operate railways in this country and who set forth very cogent reasons why that section should be enacted'. The railways of the larger grade are standardized with certain appliances and equipment, and the railway men are forced to study the rules and to understand the operation of all these various appliances and equipment, and become habituated to the use of them to such an extent that the operation of trains so standardized with such equipment become second nature to the operatives. If this Parliament, in its unwisdom, were to cut [DOT] out this salutary enactment, which was inserted for the express purpose of preserving the lives and the bodies of the railway operatives from death and accident, I think they would be doing a great injustice to those men. I am under the opinion that the minister is pursuing a most unhappy course in attempting to grant some species of favour to railways and tramways of a local nature and character at the expense of the men who operate the great standard systems of the country. What will happen in the event of the section in question being cut out? Where the operation of the standardized railway forces the men to go on to other railways that are not so standardized-railways which the law does not require to have the standardized equipment -they are thrown into a new style of operating trains where the appliances may not, and often are not, present. Through habit, they look for certain appliances, levers and aids to the operation of the train, having been habituated to the use of them, but they find them lacking and an accident
happens. It does seem to me, Sir, that the minister is going at this matter in a rather left handed way. Why not let the section stand and be universal in its application to the standardized railways and put in a proviso that this section shall not apply to railways of a merely local character, railways that are not such as would ordinarily come under the operations of the Railway Board. In that way, the difficulty is overcome. The amendment that I would suggest would be to this effect:
This section shall not apply to railways or tramways operated under a .provincial charter, or otherwise of a local nature, not coming under the provisions of the Railway Board.
If you adopt an amendment of this nature you preserve in the statute that benefit to the men which I have described, and you relieve from the operation of the statute these railways of a local character and nature.
1 oppose the Bill most strongly, knowing that the section as it stands is salutary and should not be amended, and I hope this committee will refuse to pass the Bill.

I wish to concur in every word uttered by the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy). Paragraph (c) of section 6 of the Railway Act was enacted after mature consideration and after the representatives of the railway employees from one end of Canada to the other and of the railway companies had discussed the matter fully before the special committee and before the Railway Board. What the hon. member for North Perth has said with regard to the danger that would be constantly arising from the use of non-standardized equipment if the railways were not under the jurisdiction of the Railway Board is true in every particular. And we can go further-i't is not only a case ot the railway empoyees being called upon to go from a standard railway on to a nonstandard railway, but the equipment of the non-standard railways is constantly being used" on the standard railways, the conditions of railway service making that absolutely necessary. What the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) has said with regard to special legislation dealing with particular cases is perfectly true, but this is being used in the wrong direction. Instead of enacting special legislation, as the hon. member for North Perth has suggested, to take care of some local situation that may arise on a street railway, the efforts of railway employees extending over a period of ten years to secure this legislation are going

to be thrown into the discard simply that relief may be given to a street railway at Vancouver or some other point where a condition has arisen that was not foreseen. It seems to me that the suggestion made by the hon. member for North Perth is perfectly logical; if any local situation demands that some exception should be made, let us deal with it in that way.
Hear, hear.

But after the railway committee of this House for three consecutive sessions, having had the representatives of the railway companies and of the employees before them, and having recommended this legislation for the preservation of the life and limbs of railway employees, it seems to me to be perfectly illogical for us to cast it aside simply to relieve some local situation.
'Mr. CAHILL: I move an amendment-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Just a moment, Mr. Chairman. I appreciate the force of what is said as to the value of .this clause if it is effective in the interests of railway employees. But I do not seem to have succeeded in getting the attention of hon. members to what I said with reference to the question of dealing with these matters by general disposition. As II remarked, there are two objections to this legislation: In the first place, it covers too much. We might relieve that objection by an amendment withdrawing tramways and so forth, as has been suggested; but there would remain this situation. As I said, it is a very serious question whether by a clause of that kind we can say that all railways, purely local otherwise, which are leased to or operated by railways under the legislative authority of this Parliament are works for the general advantage of Canada, and thereby bring them under our authority. The question arises : Does the British North America Act empower Parliament by a general declaration to say that all railways-taking that as one particular kind of work-that answer to a particular description are works for the general advantage of Canada? Or was not the purpose of that Act rather to enable Parliament, exercising its judgment with respect to each particular work, to declare it a work, if it found sufficient reason, for the general advantage of Canada? That question has never been categorically passed upon by the courts, but it was raised in connection with a section of a former Railway Act which provided that every railway that crossed a railway, which latter railway
tMr. Nicholson.]
was under the legislative authority of Parliament, was a work for the general advantage of Canada, and therefore fell under the legislative authority of Parliament. ,hat legislation was subsequently repealed, but it was claimed that in virtue of that Act certain local railways that crossed what I may call Dominion railways were withdrawn from the control of provincial authority. When that case reached the Privy Council the judges there said that they did not find it necessary 'to determine that question because the particular legislation under which it had arisen had been repealed. But they certainly were very careful to avoid recognizing that that legislation did effectively bring those local railways under the authority of this Parliament. They contented themselves with saying that even if those provincial roads had by that legislation been brought under Dominion authority, the subsequent repeal of the legislation left them where they originally were. I commend that to the consideration of the committee. If in face of that situation any considerable portion of the committee is still of the opinion that we had better rely upon this uncertain general legislation rather than get rid of it, leaving ourselves free to attain the object desired to be attained in a way which will certainly attain it, that is, by particular declarations in regard to particular roads,-if the committee prefer that, I have no desire at this stage of the session [DOT] to insist upon this legislation. It has been brought forward at the present moment only to meet what is a very acute situation relative to this particular case, and because the conditions of this particular case have drawn attention to the fact that in all probability there must be quite a few similar cases throughout the country, and have made it clear that at all events this section in its present form is too broad. However, as I have said, if that does not satisfy hon. members, and they still feel that they ought to oppose this legislation, I will not insist upon it at the present time.

In order that the committee may realize the importance of the subject which they are now discussing, may I be permitted to read paragraph (c):
Every railway or portion thereof, whether constructed under the authority of the Parliament of Canada or not, now or hereafter owned, controlled, leased, or operated by a company wholly or partly within the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada, or by a company operating a railway wholly or partly within the legislative authority of the Parlia-

merit of Canada, whether such ownership, control, or first mentioned operation is acquired or exercised by purchase, lease, agreement or other means whatsoever, and whether acquired or exercised under authority of the Parliament of Canada, or of the legislature of any province or otherwise howsoever; and every railway or portion thereof, now or hereafter so owned, controlled, leased or operated shall be deemed and is hereby declared to 'be a work for the general advantage of Canada.
When this subject was before the committee it was very fully discussed1. As the memlbeT for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) pointed out, representatives of different railway organizations appeared before the committee and strenuously opposed any important amendment of the clause as it now appears in the Bill. Take a railway like the Quebec Central, comprising about one hundred miles of line running through the province of Quebec. That railway is allowed to make whatever regulations it wishes to make with regard to the control of its rolling stock, and the workmen on that road seriously opposed the suggestion that they be placed in a different position from that occupied by workmen engaged on other roads throughout Canada. It should be a comparatively easy matter to amend this section in some way so that we should not interfere seriously with such roads in British Columbia as the Minister of Justice has mentioned. I am convincedi, however, that it would be a serious position for Parliament to take to allow this section to be expunged from the Railway Act.

If the minister has not
decided to report progress on the Bill, I would move in amendment:
That the following be substituted for section 1 of the Bill:
1. Paragraph (c) of section six of The Railway Act, 1919, chapter sixty-eight of the statutes of 1919, is hereby amended by inserting after the word " railway " in the first line thereof the words " except electrically operated railways."

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That would not help the matter out at all, as the hon. member will realize when I refer to the case of the Niagara and St. Catharines railway, which is part of the Canadian Northern system. If my hon. friend's amendment is pressed, the matter will be ten times worse than it is [DOT]* now.

We are nearing the end of the session, and having regard to the field of discussion which the Bill seems to open up, it is not the intention of the Government to insist stitongly on its passage. If it is the opinion of my hon. friend, the Minister of Justice, that nothing
very catastrophic would occur between now and the next session 'of Parliament if we do not adopt the measure now, we would facilitate business by withdrawing the Bill and going on to other business.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have twice announced my readiness to withdraw the Bill.

There seems to be an impression that this amendment was suggested or brought on for the benefit of some railway company. That is not the fact. The British Columbia Electric apparently is quite satisfied to be under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners, but the people of British Columbia, represented by the Attorney 'General of that province, as well as the cities of Vancouver and New Westminster and Burnaby arid other municipalities, are not satisfied that the control of street railwaays in the cities of interurban lines should be taken out of the hands of the Provincial Government. So that this amendment is suggested by the province and by the municipal authorities, not by any railway company. We are in this position in British Columbia: a public utilities commission, appointed by the province, has for some time been considering the question of fares in Vancouver, North Vancouver and New Westminster, on inter-urban and city street car lines. This proposed legislation was not known to the authorities of British Columbia; as hon. gentlemen will remember it was approved by a special committee. When it is said that something is going to be done heie without the knowledge of the railway brotherhood, I point out that this particular enactment which is complained about was put through without the knowledge of the provincial authorities. One of the members of the Opposition suggested that the provincial authorities should be notified and that they should have an opportunity of being heard, but they were not notified; they did not know anything about it. The Public Utilities Commissioner went on with his work until a few weeks ago, when he heard of this enactment and his inquiry has since been adjourned from time to time pending the settlement of this question. On the other hand, the B.C. Electric have submitted tariffs to the Board of Railway Commissioners and the Board is apparently going to attempt to assume jurisdiction. We have this conflict between two authorities, therefore, and the result is a great deal of unpleasantness and discontent. The people of British Columbia think that provincial rights have been and

are being interfered with without opportunity being given to them-to the provincial or municipal authorities-of being heard. I wanted to clear up that one point.
Now, very eminent counsel have expressed the definite opinion that this section is unconstitutional. If that is so, you are . going to have lawsuits. There is going to be a lawsuit in British Columbia which is bound to go straight through to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. If the opinions which have been expressed are sound, then this section is not going to do anybody any good. It is clear that under the British North America Act a declaration has to be .made in each particular case; that is, Parliament has to have its mind on the particular case in question and declare a particular railroad to be one for the general advantage of Canada. Now, that section is bad, and if this amendment is passed, Parliament can take up the case of the Quebec railroad or any other railroad which it desires to bring under its jurisdiction.
The Act says distinctly that any one railway may be declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada.

That is where the
constitutional question comes in; that is where this legislation is absolutely bad. I .speak on the authority of an eminent counsel when I say that this section is going to be declared ultra vires of this Parliament. It will not do the brotherhoods any good-

It will do them good
in connection with other roads.

If it is unconstitutional, it will not do anybody good. This is a public question. I repeat that this legislation is brought on not by the B.C. Electric or by any other railway company, but by the provincial and municipal authorities of British Columbia.
