speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
BILL, TO AMEND AN ACT IN AID OF [DOT] PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION PROHIBITING THE SALE OR USE OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 27, to amend an Act in aid of provincial

legislation prohibiting the sale or use of intoxicating liquors.

Mr. Speaker, before
you put the question-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The mover of the motion has the first right to speak provided that he desires to exercise that right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think that this Bill, if honourable gentlemen recollect the explanation given when it was introduced, calls, perhaps, for very little further on my part at the present moment. This Bill is an amendment to the Act in aid of provincial legislation prohibiting or restricting the sale or use of intoxicating liquors, which was passed in 1916. It will be remembered that that Act, in substance, prohibits the importation, the sending or bringing into any province of intoxicating liquors to be used in violation of the law of that province. The present Bill is designed to extend that prohibition to the manufacture of intoxicating liquor-and, in consequence, prohibiting the manufacture of intoxicating liquor-for the purpose of its being used in violation of the law of any province. The draftsman, in drafting the Bill as it is before the House, did not quite grasp the purpose that was desired, and, therefore, the Bill as printed enacts this prohibition of manufacture of intoxicating liquor, the manufacturer:
knowing or intending that such intoxicating liquor will or shall be thereafter dealt with in violation of the law of the province in which such intoxicating liquor is manufactured. -
That wording would limit this legislation by making it applicable only to a particular province. The section should read, and I purpose moving so to amend it when we get into committee:
To he thereafter dealt with in violation of the law of any province.
When we get into committee, I also purpose moving an amendment providing for the method of disposal of liquor that has been seized as having been dealt with in violation of the Act. As will be seen, this measure adopts no new principle, but merely extends the principle of the Act that it amends so as to make the rule, which the Act lays down as applicable to importation, applicable to. manufacture also, and it strikes at no liquor except such as is to be used in violation of the law of a province.

Some time ago I served notice of an amendment to Bills. Nos. 26 and 27, but since doing so I have had a conver-

sation with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty). I understand him to recognize that whatever, under these Bills, would [DOT]apply to a provincial referendum on the subject of intoxicating liquors would apply equally to any subject of referendum regarding which .a province may make a request-with, of course, the usual reservation in such cases. This recognizes the general principle of a referendum with Federal aid where necessary and requested. I am content with that, and I would therefore ask leave to withdraw my amendment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has merely given notice of an amendment, and therefore, no withrdawal is required.

I do not desire to make any objection to the provisions of Bill No. 27 in fact, I believe the provisions as contained in this Bill are a
4 p.m. proper exercise of the powers vested in this Parliament, that any legislation along this line should be enacted by this Parliament upon which the responsibility rests and that such powers should not be transferred to any other Parliament or legislative body. Nevertheless, I do not want to be taken as in any sense consenting to what I consider a violation of the principle established in this Bill by Bill No. 26, which is to follow.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, .and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Nesbitt in the Chair.
On section 1-manufacturing intoxicants, knowing, etc., that they are to be unlawfully used, forbidden:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I move:
i That subsection (al) he amended by striking out the word " the" in the third line of the subsection and by substituting the word <" any " therefor, and by striking out in the fourth and fifth lines of the subsection the [DOT]words " in which sucl\ intoxicating liquor is manufactured."
So that the eubsection will read:
'-manufactures any intoxicating liquor knowing or intending that such intoxcatiing liquor will or shall be thereafter dealt with in violation of the law of any province.
I agree with the object of the provision; but may there not be some difficulty in establishing the knowledge or intention of the manufacturer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Under the provision of the Act that is now being amended, it is on the party accused to establish that he did not sell the liquor with the "knowledge", referred to, and it will now be on him to
establish that in manufacturing it he had no knowledge of any contemplated use in violation of the law. The burden of proof will be upon the accused to establish the condition of his own knowledge. That is not an unusual provision in statutes which make it essential to an offence that an individual should have certain knowledge, and to put upon him the burden of proving what his knowledge was.
I take it the prosecution could only be instituted after the article had been dealt with in violation of provincial law?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It would be exceedingly difficult, I think, to succeed upon a prosecution where that had happened. If one were in a position to know, before the thing had actually been carried out, that that was the intention, he might institute his prosecution. I think it is comparatively easy for the party accused to demonstrate his innocence of any knowledge that it was going to be used in violation of the law. Now, with regard to sub-section 2, of section 1, I move that it be amended so as to make section 4 of the Act, which is amended by this sub-section, read:
On any prosecution for the violation of section one of this Act the accused person shall be *deemed to have known or intended that such intoxicating liquor would be thereafter dealt *with in violation of the law of any province in which such liquor was manufactured or of any 'other province into which such intoxicating liquor was sent, shipped, taken, brought, carried or imported, unless he proves that he had good reason for believing that the intoxicating liquor would only be dealt with in a lawful manner.
Would it not be better legislation to repeal the law and then reenact it in concrete form?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps that would be better, to substitute for the present subsection 2 of this Act the following provision: "Section 4 of the said Act is repealed and the following is substituted therefor" and so on. That is, to reproduce section 4 with the added words which I have just suggested. The effect will be that section 4 will in future read so as to cover the case of manufacture as well as the case of sending or transporting the liquor.
Having heard the explanation of the minister, is it your pleasure that the clause as proposed be amended ?

I do not wish to obstruct the minister's Bill in any way, but as a practicing barrister I must say that I am

not in favour of that part of it that casts the burden of the evidence to be adduced at the trial upon the accused. It is not necessary for me to say that the Supreme Court has held that the violation of the Temperance law is a criminal offence. When we are dealing with the question of selling liquor in violation of the law, we are dealing with something which is a crime, and the principle of British justice has been that every man has been presumed to be innocent until he is proved guilty. Now we establish a crime in connection with this Act and we say at once that he is guilty until he proves his innocence. I wish to put myself on record as opposed to that system of trial in whatever form it may come up. I think the temperance people, myself amongst them, should be satisfied to be left in the same position exactly as any other man who has to prove a crime. They should be left to prove that an accused man -is guilty. I think that would be better temperance than going the length of putting a man on his trial and declaring him to be guilty before the evidence is heard. As an old lawyer who has had a great deal to do with the criminal law, I want to put myself on record as being opposed to this change in the well-established principle of our criminal law.

I quite agree with the remarks of the hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) in that regard. The decisions in the Ontario Court of Appeal are altogether in line with the argument advanced. In the cases of Regina v. Baird, and Regina v. Sproule, the Court of Appeal, after due deliberation held that no conviction under the Canada Temperance Act could be made without positive and affirmative testimony, and that negative testimony was not sufficient. It was held that it was the duty of the prosecution to establish by evidence that was credible and worthy of belief that the act complained of had been committed. I do not think it is fair to turn upside down the well-known principle of which the hon. gentleman has spoken and to provide that a man placed on trial should be required to prove his innocence. It is the duty of the State to bring home to the accused the act with which he is charged. The principle of the law which presumes a man to be innocent until proved guilty should be upheld in the public interest and to safeguard the liberty of the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In the first place, the principle has been established, in the Act

which we are amending, and we are only extending the 6ame principle to cover the addition that this amendment makes to the Act. The second thing that I would like to say is that this does not put the burden of proof in reference to any act upon the accused; but when it shall have been proved- that he manufactured* the liquor, or that he sold the liquor, and it comes to be a question of whether or not he knew the purpose for which it was to be used, this will put the burden of proof upon him-if you can call it a burden to prove what his own knowledge was. These are facts that are within the knowledge of the accused and which it is particularly easy for an innocent man to clear up. It is a very general provision, where the guilt is made to depend upon knowledge on the part of the accused to throw upon him the burden of proof as to what his knowledge was. That is the only burden of proof that is put upon him.
Section as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I beg to move to amend the Act by adding a clause as clause 3. This will have the effect of amending section 4A of the Act.
This is a section, 4A, providing for the seizure of all liquor that has been the object of a violation of the law and declaring how that liquor is to be dealt with. The purpose of the section to be added is to make provision for dealing with liquor that has been dealt with in contravention of this law and where the owner cannot be found. It has been found by experience that when liquor has been seized under circumstances that clearly indicate that it has been sent into the province in violation of the law, nobody comes forward to claim it, and you cannot find any person against whom you can get an order made in regard to the disposition of the liquor. It is proposed by thi's section to make provision for disposing of the liquor under these circumstances. The new clause is proposed to be added after section 4A and is as follows:
(1) When any intoxicating liquor is seized and brought before any judge of the sessions of the peace, recorder, police magistrate, stipendiary magistrate, two justices of the peace or any magistrate having the power or authority of two or more justices of the peace, in pursuance of the provisions of this Act, and the consignor or consignee or owner thereof or person entitled thereto or claiming the same cannot be ascertained, and if no person establishes a claim to the possession of such intoxicating liquor within a period of fifteen days after the seizure thereof as aforesaid, or within such extended time as the judge of the sessions of

the peace, recorder, police magistrate, stipendiary magistrate, two justices of the peace or magistrate having the power or authority of two or more justices of the peace, may allow, or as may otherwise be allowed by any competent tribunal, then the judge of the sessions of the peace, recorder, police magistrate, stipendiary magistrate, two justices of the peace or magistrate having the power or authority of two or more justices of the peace who issue! the warrant in execution of which such intoxicating liquor was seized, or, in the case of the death, absence or inability to act of such judge of the sessions of the peace, recorder, police magistrate stipendiary magistrate, two justices of the peace or magistrate having the power or authority of two or more justices of the peace, any other judge of the sessions of the peace, recorder, police magistrate, stipendiary magistrate, two justices of the peace or magistrate having the power or authority of two or more justices of the peace, may adjudge and declare such intoxicating liquor, together with all kegs, barrels, cases, 'boxes, bottles, packages, containers and other receptacles of any kind whatever found containing the same, be forfeited to the Crown.
(2) As soon as any intoxicating liquor and the receptacles containing the same are forfeited -to the Crown, the judge of the sessions of the peace, recorder, police magistrate, stipendiary magistrate, two justices of the peace or magistrate having the power or authority of two ot more justices of the peace, by whom such forfeiture is adjudged and declared shall immediately transmit to the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue a notice in writing specifying the quantities and descriptions of the intoxicating liquor so forfeited, and shall order that such intoxicating liquor shall immediately be deposited in a Customs bonding warehouse within the province wherein such intoxicating liquor is forfeited as aforesaid, to be disposed of as the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue may direct.
What method of disposition of the liquor would that contemplate?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I presume the minister might dispose of it by destroying it, or seeing that it was used for legitimate purposes. I think the provision is so worded as to be in accordance with the provisions of the* law dealing with liquors that are forfeited under the Inland Revenue Act. We put these liquors into the hands of the Minister of Inland Revenue to be disposed of as he may determine, and I doubt not he will dispose of them in the same manner in which articles of the sarnie kind forfeited under the Inland Revenue Act are disposed of.
M^. McKENZTE: I do not quite understand the limits of the jurisdiction of the magistrate or the authority that is authorized to deal with this liquor. In Nova Scotia we have a provincial law which is very much akin to this provision. That is, if liquors are found anywhere in the province and nobody claims them within
thirty days after they are received, an order can be made by the magistrate who issues the warrant, or the summons, to deal with them as any other liquors that are illegally used under the Nova Scotia Temperance Act are dealt with. That is very plain. But the procedure proposed here would appear to rather conflict with it. I do not quite understand why the order can only be made by the man who tried the case. There must be an information laid under proper jurisdiction with respect to this liquor. I would understand that the man who tried the offence should make the decree or order to dispose of the liquor; but does the minister say that the clause means that one magistrate may try the case and declare the liquor forfeited, and that none of the other courts mentioned may issue an order for the destruction of the liquor?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In principle it is the
magistrate who issues the warrant who makes the order with regard to this liquor, but if he should die or be unable to act, some other magistrate having similar jurisdiction may make the order.

I did not at first catch the nature of the provision. If it is, as the minister explains, it is all right.
Ssubsection 1 of amendment agreed to.

The
next is sub-clause 2-disposal of forfeited liquor, as read by the minister. Shall that carry?

There is one provision
that I have been trying to grasp, I do not think it is exactly right as at present worded. I do not see how a man could be said to be claiming a thing when the officers of the law cannot find him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The clause reads that
if the officers cannot find the owner, " or any person entitled thereto, or claiming the same"-that is to say if they cannot find anybody who claims it. and so on.

I think the clause is
rather unhappily expressed.
Subsection 2 of amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What particular conference does that item refer to?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
The Conference that was held at Ottawa and which my hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) attended.
Department of Labour-Amount required to defray expenses of Canadian delegates and advisers, to International Labour Conference at Washington, $2'5,000.

I do not know that the doctrine of Cabinet solidarity could be pushed so far as that. I have no knowledge of what has taken place at the Conference, except what I gather from the newspapers. But different sides are represented, labour and employers, and it is natural that there should be some difference of opinion between them, and we can only expect our delegates to use their best judgment as to how they shall vote.
 *

Might we not have some explanation as to what is expected to be accomplished by the Conference? I am aware that the Conference had its origin in the Peace Treaty, but I really think the House has had very little explanation regarding the Conference itself.

My hon. friend will see if he has read the newspapers-[DOT] and I know he has-that the Conference is at present discussing the forty-eight or forty-four hour week. The object aimed at is to get international agreement with reference to the weekly hours of labour. That object, if it can be gained, has certainly very great advantages. In fact, it is hoped that as a result of the deliberations of the Conference on the range of subjects connected with labour that an international agreement may be reached thereon. I am sorry that, not being at the head of the Department of (Labour, I have no special knowledge of the proceedings and can give my hon. friend only a general idea of what the Conference is expected to accomplish.

I am not putting my
question in any critical spirit.
No.

I _ realize that these
labour problems are of such vast importance that we should try to find solutions for them. The Conference, of course, has neither executive nor legislative power in itself; whatever it might do could only be made effective by subsequent legislation on the part of the nations concerned.
~Sir GEORGE FOSTER: I think'so.
I wish I could see any reasonable hope of such international agreement as my hon. friend suggests. The object of the Conference is a good one at all events.
We must make progress by degrees.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Does the
Acting Prime Minister know how much longer the proceedings at Washington are likely to last?

When you'get
a meeting of labour men belonging to one nationality, and try to make an estimate as to how long they will talk, I think it will be admitted that you have a pretty difficult problem on your hands; but when you consider that the deliberations will be participated in by representa-

tives of twenty-eight different nationalities and that many different languages will be spoken, it is beyond my power to make an estimate of how long it will take them to come to an absolute conclusion.

I understand that the *law officers here have expressed the opinion that any legislation affecting the length of the workman's day or the number of hours of labour per day is a provincial question; and if I remember correctly, the Prime Minister made a statement, to that effect in the House last session. Even if this conference should decide on an eight-hour day, then, any Canadian enactment in that regard would have to be made through the different provincial legislatures. May I ask whether there was any consultation with the respective provincial governments concerning the appointment of delegates to attend this conference on behalf of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The provinces, of course, were not entitled to delegates as provinces, but the different Provincial Governments were asked to send, and I believe all did [DOT]send, representatives selected from their officials, in some instances provincial minister of the Crown, to accompany the representatives of Canada as experts and to be entitled, m the absence of the titular representative of Canada, to act in his place. The province of Quebec sent their inspector of industrial establishments, the officer who has charge of all matters connected with labour questions.
Additional amount required for the remainder of the fiscal year to defray expenses of the Director of Coal Operations and staff in Alberta, and for printing, stationery and clerical assistance, not otherwise provided for, $25,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What is the
nature of the operations that are being carried on under this head? The four items which we have been considering involve a total vote of $60,000, and all the items represent activities which are more or less outside the Department of Labour. The criticism that one hears from many sides is that the Department of Labour is not really carrying on the work for which it was established; that it is delegating the greater part of the work to commissions and outside organizations. A great deal of public money is being spent on work which is supposedly part of the work of the Labour Department but which, in reality, is being carried' on by bodies wholly independent of that department. This last item seems to be of that nature.

Perhaps it would be nearer the truth-I do not .say it offensively-to say that the department is carrying on all the old-time activities and is also stretching out in new directions. Really these services are activities which have been proceeding during the war period under the War Measures Act. As the War Measures Act will in part, cease when the ratifications of peace are deposited some time this month, it was felt that the charging of these items to demobilization account under the War Measures Act could not be continued. This particular item arose out of the utter disorganization of the British Columbia coal mines this side of the mountains. These were put under the control of a director who has been working for over two years. He is doing the work very efficiently as a public service, but we must, of course, provide for the necessary expenses. I assure my honourable friend that this work has been very successful in mitigating the labour troubles in that district and in ensuring a more or less continued operation of the mines. I believe that the mines are presently operating with afhity and with success.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The strike in the United States has not affected the mines in this country?
Not as yet; we are very hopeful that it will not.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister remarked that after the ratifications of the Treaty of Peace had been deposited in Paris, the War Measures Act would be suspended "in part". In what respect will the Act be continued?

I used the words "in part" as a cautionary measure. I am not a lawyer and I am not sure how long the War Measures Act may remain in operation, having regard to the fact that we are still in a state of war with certain enemy countries; and that will be the condition until all the different treaties are agreed upon and finally ratified. The Treaty with Bulgaria has not yet been ratified, although it is well up to the point of agreement, but the treaties with Hungary and with Turkey are no further than the period of negotiation. I am not the Minister of Justice; therefore it is well that I should put in the words "in part".

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does the minister not think that we ought to try to get out of the state of war as soon as we can?
Absolutely so.

Is this Director of Coal
operations in Alberta at present directing the distribution of coal?

His duty was to direct the distribution of coal, arrange satisfactory wages and their payment, and determine what the cost of coal should he to the consumer having regard to the expenses of operation. In fact, his powers were wide; they gave him directive authority over both operators and miners.

The reason I asked the question was that at many points in Saskatchewan there are no cars. In some places even schools are being closed. The Government should take some steps at once because the state of affairs is very serious owing t'o the extreme weather conditions in the West at the present time. In fact, I had a telegram from Kerr-Robert yesterday saying that the people had no oars; that the schools were closed, and that there was dire need of fuel.
The Government is keeping track of the coal situatioh in the West as well as in the East.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: A telegram was received from the Provincial Treasurer of Saskatchewan yesterday in reference to the coal situation that had arisen in Saskatchewan on account of the very cold weather during the last three or four weeks. That telegram has been transmitted to the Labour Department, and I understand that the Labour Department has got in touch with Mr. Armstrong who is in charge of this work. I have no doubt at all that he will take the matter in hand with a view of seeing what can he done. This is a purely temporary situation and has arisen as a result of very cold weather conditions extending 'over a short period.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I should like to say a word or two with reference to the shortage of cars. For some time I have been receiving telegrams from the West complaining about the shortage 'of cars for the shipment of hay, coal and wheat. That has been going on not only for the last few weeks, but for a year. The reason for the shortage is this. In the past there was generally a surplus of American cars in Canada, but the American Government since it has had charge of the situation, has been keeping our cars in the United States and there have been in the neighbourhood of 20,000 more Canadian box cars in the United States than American cars in Canada. Yesterday the way in which
[Sir George Foster. 1
the car situation stood was this: There are now located in the United States 1,830 Canadian livestock cars and 43,661 Canadian box cars, to offset which we have only 158 livestock cars and 21,240 box cars of United States railroads in Canada. In other words, yesterday there were 22,000 Canadian box cars in the United States over and above the number of American cars in Canada. I have been taking the matter up by wire in the strongest possible terms with Mr. Walter D. Hines, representative of the American railways. The railways themselves have been doing everything possible to get those cars over here, but we have not yet been successful in reducing that great difference. We are still continuing our efforts, and perhaps it might be well to read a telegram that I received yesterday and that will show exactly the position I have taken as regards the shortage of empty cars in the West. I took the matter up with the Canadian Railway War Board on account of the complaints from the West about not getting cars for livestock, and this is the reply I received:

know that the Railway Department, the Canadian Pacific, the Grand Trunk and the Canadian National railways have for a long time been taking every means possible to get those cars back. But Walter D. Hines, who is in charge of this, seems utterly to ignore all appeals we make in the interest of humanity and doing justice to our country to give back to us the cars to which we are entitled.
Would it not be feasible for the Minister of Railways to increase the per diem rate at which those cars are now being charged, to double or treble it, if necfessary?

speechtext: Yes.

He was decidedly out of order in speaking about what happened in the other Chamber. Now, to come back to the item under discussion. I understood from the minister that the director of coal operations was doing his work as a matter of public service, receiving no remuneration. I desire to register an emphatic protest against our being asked to pass an item of $25,000 in the absence of more detailed information. If we were asked to pass items in connection -with any regular department, the Government would place before us the number of clerks employed and the salary of each, and would give more details 'than we have in regard to this somewhat extraneous work undertaken by the Department Of Labour. I submit that when work is done outside of the ordinary functions of a department there should be full and accurate information 'as to how the money that is asked for is to be spent. This item does not tell us whether the Director of Coal Operations is to get any salary or not. Perhaps he is, but we have no information to that effect. We are not told the number of his staff and what their salaries are. The minister says that he is not a lawyer, but to poor and honest members of the legal profession $25,000 is



a considerable sum, and I repeat with emphasis that we should not be asked to pass this item without a great deal more in the way of detail than we have.

Probably the busiest man in Alberta is the gentleman to whom reference is made in this discussion. In the province of Alberta we have one-twelfth of the world's coal, although few .members realize that fact. We have hundreds of mines, and during the war we were obliged to depend to a great extent on alien labour. These people were, to my mind, somewhat unreasonable in their demands for wages, and victuals the richness of which would heretofore have spoilt their stomachs they spurned and grumbled at. They say now that they must have tomatoes out of season, green onions in winter, and so forth, and Mr. Armstrong has had considerable work to do as a mediator. I can assure the hon. member that he has been a very busy man. During the last four years we have had trouble continuously, always on the verge of strike, and these conditions create a good deal of work for the director and his staff. He has a Staff in the city of Calgary, and they coveT a territory from the city of Edmonton to Lethbridge, and in the Crowsnest Pass. And it costs money to travel. No sooner is a disturbance settled "in one end of the country then they have to journey to another. Altogether, from the nature of the work that these men have to carry on, I would say that the estimate is a very conservative one.

The member who has so kindly given this information to the committee quite ignores the purport of my remarks. I am not saying that this estimate is either too little or too much, nor do I say that the work of the Director is either good or bad. I do not know anything about the matter, and I merely suggest to the committee, quite properly as I think, that if we are asked to pass an estimate of $25,000 in connection- with this work we should know just what it is for. Is it for salaries or indemnities, for stationery, or for what else? I think we should have more details. Certainly, more information would be given us if the work were done under the department itself; and I think, a fortiori, that in this instance we are all the more justified in asking for detailed information.
A what?
A fortiori,-a very usual term.
In Assiniboia?
And also in Carleton, N. B.

My hon. friend, on principle, is quite right. I have h(?ard the same appeal made just as fervently as he has made it to-night on innumerable occasions, and by members on each side of the House alternately.
You never made it yourself?	.

Generally the
protestations come louder from the Opposition than from the Government side of the House, for which I suppose there is a natural reason. Now, my hon. friend, being satisfied that his principles are right, and having made his protest, is faced with this fact, that the Minister of Labour is not at the present time here and that I am acting pro tern, with an imperfect knowledge of his department. If 'the hon. member, however, will take my moral and other responsibilities as well as those of the Minister of Labour himself, for a fair and just expenditure of the small sum which is required, and allow the item to go through, he will have an easy conscience and. will sleep well, and we shall be able to proceed to the consideration of other items. Now. could not my hon. friend stretch his good nature far enough to allow'the item to pass?

A soft answer turneth
away wrath.
Dominion Lands and Parks-Amount required to provide relief by way of necessary supplies of food, clothing, fuel, etc., also fodder for animals to needy settlers of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan by co-operation and agreement with the provincial governments or otherwise, and under regulations to be made by the Governor in Council, $2,000,000.

I had expected that this
amount would be larger and I am therefore not at all surprised that at least $2,000,000 should be asked for. Like every one else, I like to see the necessity for relief removed. I understood either the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Cal-der) or the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) to say that negotiations had been opened with the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta looking to the establishment of an irrigation scheme in that part of' the country to remove the ever recurring demand for relief there. I would like to ask if they have started these negotiations, and, if so, what progress they are making. It seems to me that something of that kind should be done in a very comprehensive manner.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Dominion's part in what my hon. friend (Mr. Cowan) calls negotiations has already been pretty well performed; at all events, it has been in progress of performance "'for many years. The Dominion Government has for a period of many years-indeed, dating back to the first of the century, or close to that time-undertaken the survey work in connection with irrigation projects. Back as far as 1894 control was asserted by this Parliament over the surface waters of the three prairie provinces. Growing out of that control, which was necessarily a Dominion jurisdiction, the Dominion Government established a system of surveys with a view to ascertaining what were legitimate, and from the business standpoint likely successful, irrigation projects. As a result a survey was made, followed by actual engineering supervision of any construction enterprise entered into, and there has been very considerable progress made in the way of actual irrigation projects in these three provinces.'
That has largely been, of course, by the Canadian Pacific Company on the one hand and by what is now known as the Canada Land and Irrigation Company on the other. The latter is a combination of what were * formerly three companies engaged in the same work. The Canadian Pacific irrigation schemes now embrace, not a considerable area having regard to the; amount of land that needs irrigation, but quite an area. Many farmers in Western Canada now are on Canadian Pacific irrigated land and doing remarkably well. The Canada Land and Irrigation Company have encountered many reverses and delays. It is, perhaps, more correct to say that the companies now comprised in the Canada Land and Irrigation Company encountered these reverses. The war came on and the whole investment of these concerns seemed to be at the point of being wrecked. The Government, however, came to the assistance of the companies by way of a loan, the agreement for which is of a rather complicated nature. The Government are amply secured and the agreement which was made has. vindicated itself abundantly, the consequence being that the whole of the enterprise and of the work already done were conserved, and now the monies advanced by the Government are in process of being repaid. The Canada Land and Irrigation Company, under Mr. Hays' management, has made most substantial progress and is now at the point where there does not seem to be any good reason why quite an area of the land that they seek to irri-
123i
gate will not be in shape for sale and for actual irrigation next spring.
All this work is supervised by the Irrigation Branch of the Department of the Interior. No land is allowed to be included in any system of irrigation and no land is allowed to be sold until the whole scheme of irrigation has been approved and until, as regards each separate parcel, the soil content and the plans of the company as to how much of the land is irrigable and can be used to advantage, are examined by the department. As regards the progress of these two concerns, very much practical work has been done and its value is largely demonstrative of what is possible in other areas.
The Dominion Government, as a matter of policy, has taken the ground that actual irrigation construction is noi a Dominion responsibility. It is a provincial responsibility or a local responsibilty of some kind. We have met with some resistance in pressing that principle but I think I am not going beyond the mark in saying that the principle is now accepted on the part of the province of Alberta any way and I do not know that it is seriously resisted on the part of the province of Saskatchewan. There is no immediate difficulty in the case of Manitoba. The government of the province of Alberta are naturally anxious that they do not become involved in responsibilities until they know the exact nature of the project that they are asked to endorse. They are anxious also that the Dominion Government continue to press on this survey work with the utmost possible speed and that the Dominion's imprirualur foV each separate project be given just as soon as the information can with the greatest rapidity be obtained.. That is being done. I think I can say that we have spared nothing in the way of expense so long as we have felt that the money was being properly expended to hasten this survey work. Because we have done that we have made a great deal of progress. Our part of the contract, if you can call it a contract, is well advanced. I do not think there is any reason to fear that the part that must be taken by the provinces will not readily be taken just as soon as the projects are at the stage where each province will have to decide what it is going to do about it.
In the matter of bringing about a solution of the dry area difficulty in western Canada by irrigation, let us not deceive ourselves. There does not seem to be any possibility that the supply of water that will be avail-

able for Canada from the rivers that are within reach of irrigable land, or rather land that is drought stricken, will be anything like sufficient to take care of all the land that ought to be irrigated. We will just have to use that supply of water to the utmost possible advantage and to see that none is diverted where it will do less good than it might have done if it had been directed somewhere else. That is a problem and a responsibility that the Dominion Government must shoulder and is shouldering. It is very probable that only a fraction of the land that would be much better of irrigation in western Canada can be irrigated by the available water supply.
Before that item is passed I would like some information in regard' to this expenditure. When will it be available to the settlers?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is the real point. The arrangements made this year have taken some time but there has been nothing in the way of a hitch. There is an agreement between the Dominion Government and the province of Alberta and I believe that with the province of Saskatchewan there is a separate agreement. The arrangement is this: In 1915 the Dominion Government took the whole- responsibility of relieving the needs of the drought-stricken areas where actual relief had to be furnished to keep the people alive, to keep them supplied with essentials until spring and with seed. That responsibility .was assumed both as regards homesteaders who had not received their patents and as regards owners and it involved a very great outlay. In 1915 the conditions were somewhat analogous to what they have been in 1919. In
1917	in these regular drought areas there was only what might be called a half harvest-no, there was not even that. In
1918	there was a failure

not total, but almost-and very considerable hardship. In 1919 there is a complete failure and very great hardship. With these three reverses, one following on the other, we have conditions that parallel the conditions of 1915. It did not seem right to me that the Dominion treasury should meet this expenditure entirely, and I am glad to say that the provinces have met us in a fair spirit and we have come to an arrangement. It is agreed that where expenditures must be made they shall be made by the provinces and through provincial administrative machinery. They supply the organization to do it, see where it is essential, and provide for it where that is the ease. Wherever they make the actual outlay for relief,, we bear half

and they bear the other half. In the case of unpatented homesteads, they take the lien in our favour and pass it on to us; where it is patented l^nd they take the lien in their own favour. Whenever they collect money on these securities they give us half and when we collect money we give them half. They are credited with half of our collections and we with half of theirs, so that if all the money is collected we will each get our part; if there is a loss we both share it. That is the Whole principle of the transaction.
Mr. ARGUE.: Are these payments to be made in one year or two?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The payments will be
due in one year. I am far from saying they will be made in one year; they never have been. We have lost veky little but it takes a long while for the payments to be made.
I think the provincial government this year are keeping down advances for relief to the minimum. We know that to be their intention; they are going to confine the relief given to certain staple necessities and to nothing else-that is what I am informed. They lose one-half of whatever is lost, so I think that is sufficient security for us.

That is not the situation
to which I wish to draw attention. Take the drought-stricken areas where the merchants in the villages -and towns have been carrying these farmers through for the entire year. ,When it came to the end of the year and they should have been paying their bills, they had not got a dollar for the purpose. If the Government lends them money to carry on for another year, and then request the re-payment of the whole of it next year, the .merchant who carries these people on his books must continue to do so for another twelve months. I would like to know if the Government could not collect fifty .per cent of the indebtedness in 1920 and allow the farmer this year to pay off fifty per cent of his indebtedness to the merchant who has carried him?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think the
Government is likely to get the advantage of the local merchant in the collection; we never do. The local merchant will get his fifty per cent all right, Anyway, under the plan that will be in vogue now,, that will have to be taken care of by the provincial government. Under the arrangement they will look after the re-payment in the case of -all unpatented homesteads, which class is variously estimated at from ten to seven-

teen per cent of the total number who need relief.
Who supplies the seed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The provincial government, through the municipalities supplies the seed altogether for patented homesteads, and we supply it for unpatented homesteads.

Is the distribution to be made through the municipal councils? The reason I asli is that if it be done that way unnecessary expense will be avoided. The farmers at the present time are in poor circumstances and I would therefore suggest that in the interest of economy the distribution be made through the municipal councils.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We bear no expense at all ourselves, but of course the expense has increased. What the province is doing is this: in the main they guarantee the municipalities, and the municipalities provide the essential necessities themselves, under the control of the province, the province guaranteeing the municipality at the bank and holding- the municipality responsible. The only time we come in in such cases is when the province is called upon to pay by reason of its guarantee. If the province is not called upon to pay, then we have nothing to pay. In Alberta, especially, there is very little organized territory in the municipalities as yet, so that in that province the arrangement cannot be carried out in that way. In that case they simply use the regular provincial officers; but where they have a municipality they use it.
It would be interesting if the minister could tell us what percentage of the last advance made in this fashion has been returned?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There never was an advance made in this fashion. The advance to which the hon. gentleman doubtless refers was made in 1915. I cannot recall the exact figures but I will give them approximately and as closely as I can. In 1915, $12,300,000 was advanced for relief and seed grain. Of that amount about $7,500,000 was for seed grain and about $5,000,000, for relief. The total amount returned at the last inquiry I made was about $9,500,000. That includes seed payments. There have been more returns made since, so that there would be about $3,000,000 and interest outstanding. The larger portion of that was for relief; in that class of cases we had to
take a last lien: in the case of seed grain we took a first lien.

In addition to what the
minister has said I may explain that there is no doubt about the security in the case of these loans, because the Government has taken a first lien on the land.
What provision is being made for the issue of grain for next spring?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My present intention
is to recommend that we follow the course that was pursued last spring. That is, where the seed is to be furnished to unpatented homesteads we arrange to have our agents recommend each individual case to the bank designated by the homesteader. The homesteader selects his own seed and gets his money from the bank at a rate of seven per cent, giving his note and his lien, and then we guarantee a return of the principal and five per cent interest.

Is it the intention of
the Government to give assistance to the needy settlers again this spring?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Does the honourable
gentleman mean for seed?
Yes, for seed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Entirely as regards
unpatented lands. Where it is essential we will have to see it is done, and I recommend its being done on the same plan that was adopted this year.

The hon. member asked as to the number of men settled in each province. I am not sure that I have that information before me, but, as might he expected, the three western provinces have the largest number. When I last examined the figures the province of Alberta had the Largest number, the province of Saskatchewan came next, and then Manitoba and British Columbia. Where are the men undergoing their training?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We utilize the provincial agricultural colleges mainly; but we have establish at 'Sherbrooke, Quebec, and at another eastern point training centres where we have lands leased for the purpose, and we also have men in training on farms where we supply them with a Little assistance if they are married men to support their dependents on a very limited scale,-not at all on the scale of the Civil Re-establishment Department. We do not give these men the regular agricultural college training course at all, but a practical training course of three months, in fact, just such a course as will make them useful on the land. The regular agricultural college course is intended to make a good farmer a better farmer; our course is intended to make a man who is not a farmer at all practically useful on a farm.
Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment-To carry out the recommendations of the report of the committee on Bill No. 10 (Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment), $40,000,000.

In the expenditure of this money I think the department might utilize the Soldiers' Aid Commissions in some of the provinces, especially in the way of looking after the unemployed and those who are disabled. Those commissions have been engaged in that work for three or four

years, and I am assured by the secretary of the Ontario Commission that they would be disposed to continue it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
I have already received a communication from the Soldiers' Aid Commission of Ontario to the effect that they will be willing to co-operate in every way possible. I have my doubts as to whether the expenditure of this money should be placed under a provincial organization, because after all, those commissions in the various provinces are provincial. We are providing here a fairly large sum of money and it is absolutely necessary to surround the expenditure of that money with adequate safeguards to insure its being spent for the purposes for which it is intended. The Government as yet has not had an opportunity of considering what should be done in the way of establishing the necessary administration to look after this work, but it seems to me that whatever kind of administration is established, it will have to be of such a character as to make certain that this money is used entirely for the purpose which the House had in mind when we were discussing the matter the other day.
Some suggestions have been thrown out that probably the Patriotic Fund organization might act. Personally I have very grave doubts as to the advisability of that. On the other hand, it might be that we have some existing machinery that would be able to carry on this work without duplication. All I can say to the committee at the present time is that the expenditure of this money must be guarded with the greatest possible care. I think there is no doubt in the minds of any member of the committee as to the intention of the House in approving of this suggestion. Every precaution should be taken to see that the money is not squandered or wasted in any way, and the Government has the matter under consideration and will endeavour to establish whatever machinery is necessary, or to use whatever machinery exists with those objects in view.

I am afraid that we are just a little too close to six o'clock to get through this item, because it is a very important one and we want definite information in regard to it. Is this $40,000,000 made up of an itemized statement, or is it just a guess; and is much of it to be taken up by what the minister has been prone to call commitments-how much of it goes to payments for which the department is already committed, or is it all available for

new cases that may arise? Can the minister give any general information as to how we arrive at the $40,000,000 ?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
In our report we made a series of recommendations, all involving the expenditure of money. In respect of certain items the estimate, I think, is approximately correct. For example, one ol our recommendations was that gratuities heretofore paid to members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force should be payable also to Canadians who enlisted in the Imperial forces, minus the gratuity which they received from the Imperial Government. The committee went into that fully and estimated that the cost involved in carrying out this recommendation would be in the neighbourhood of $9,000,000. The committee recommended also that we should refund the fares paid by the wives and children 'of soldiers who returned to Canada prior to the armistice. Since the armistice the Government has paid such fares and it was thought just that those who returned prior to the armistice should be treated on the same basis. We know that about 17,000 dependents returned before the armistice, and that about 34,000 have returned since. We know what the actual cost has been, and we estimate that to carry out this recommendation will involve an expenditure of about $1,000,000.
Mr. McKENZIE.: What machinery does the minister propose to establish for the purpose 'of getting at the persons he has to deal with under these items?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: There will be no difficulty about that. As soon as the announcement was made in t'he press that these two" recommendations had been made, applications commenced to come in. We have had a very voluminous correspondence with those whose dependents returned prior to the armistice. Our various soldier organizations are interested in both these questions. They all know that the committee has made that recommendation, and, as I say, applications will come in rapidly. As to the gratuities to Imperifds, the Militia Department have on record the list of all those who served in the Imperial forces; if not, they will be able to get the necessary information.

I do not think they
have such a Tecord. I had one case of an Englishman by birth who left this country and joined the Imperial forces. He was killed, and I communicated with the Government on behalf of his widow, who lives
in my constituency, with a view to their looking after her. The answer I got was that the IMilitia Department had no record of this man because he had joined on the other side.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: That may be so. They have some records here, but I have no doubt that others will have to be obtained. 1 take it, however, that every one who is entitled to this gratuity will apply for it at an early day; then jit will be simply a question of ascertaining whether or not the applicant is entitled to the payment, and, if he is, of seeing that the payment is made. That covers these itwo items. Then, the report made a series of recommendations, grouped, because of the impossibility of arriving at a definite estimate. One of our recommendations is that men undergoing medical treatment during a fairly long period in hospitals under the control o(f (the Department of 'Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment should get their clothing free. I suppose if the committee had had time they would have been able to arrive at an estimate of Ithe expenditure involved in carrying out this suggestion, but they did not take time to do that. Again, we recommended that a man whlo had been taken on the strength of Ithe vocational branch of the department and who was afterwards discharged because of the fact that he should not have been taken on should receive the pay and allowances provided for those who take vocational training. Sometimes when a man comes to Ottawa to take the training there is every indication that he is entitled to do so. There is sometimes delay in getting the necessary medical and other documents, and pending the completion of these the man may be taken on strength. Then, possibly a week 'afterwards, it may be found that the man was not entitled, under the regulations of the department, to take the training. It was decided by the committee, after hearing very full evidence on that point, that in such cases the pay and allowances should be given as I have stated. .There are hot very many cases of that kind.

1 wish to make a brief plea, before the minister proceeds any further, on behalf of a class of soldiers who at the present time do not get gratuities. I am impelled to do this because the minister said, when the report was under consideration, that the acceptance of the report would not bar the door to further suggestions. I know that the matter was considered by the committee, but I ask the minister to

consider it again. I refer to Canadian-naturalized citizens, many of 'whom had been in Canada for many years, had married * and were bringing up families here, some of them men of forty years and upwards, who when the call came rallied to the colours in the respective European countries to which they belonged. There they were fighting the battle of Canada-because the cause was a common one-in August, September, 1914. I have one case in mind of a man who was fighting the battle of Canada in the French army as early as September, 1914. That man, who for ten years had been a Canadian citizen, comes back with both hands maimed. He does not receive any gratuity. Had he been an English reservist who had re-joined his regiment in England and gone to the Continent in the British Expeditionary Force, he would have been entitled to gratuity. Why should such a distinction be drawn? I do not think that there should be a distinction, and as a matter of justice and of equitable treatment of all I would ask the minister to give the case of such soldiers further consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: That matter has received consideration and, I dare say, should receive further consideration. I wish to direct attention to one representation that was made to the committee-I am not sure that it is well founded-and that is this: that although a man came from Greece to Canada, say ten years ago and settled down here and became naturalized, he had not completely severed his Greek citizenship. If he were a Greek reservist, and Great Britain were at war with Greece, although he had become a naturalized Canadian, he -would still be subject to the call of Greece. Does the hon. member see the point?
I see the point, but-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
I understand that the
statement was made to the committee that that was true of French and Italian reservists. So long as those countries remain under a system whereby when their people go out to other parts of the world to settle they continue to carry their citizenship with them and to be subject to military law, our position in regard to such people is quite different from that in dealing with our own citizens, citizens within the British Empire. There is a distinction there.

It is a distinction for which the soldier is in no way responsible. I have in mind a French reservist who was

naturalized in 1900, who has been for many-years a voter in the county which I represent, and who at the outbreak of war, although he was a married man with half' a dozen children, immediately went over to France and took part in the war. I think it is very hard that he should not receive-the same treatment as if he were an Englishman who had enlisted.

By leave of the House I beg to move concurrence in the Senate amendments to Bill No. 18, to amend the Civil Service Act, 1918. The amendments are not very important, therefore I think we should accept them. The first amendment is on page 2. The clause as it now stands provides that if any position is abolished, the incumbent of that position is put on an eligible list for the class of position from which he was laid off. That-means that if the position is abolished, he will be eligible for appointment to the same kind of position. The Senate adds this:
Or for any other-position for which he maybe qualified.
That, I think, is fair. The next amendment provides for the elimination of the word " organization " which occurs in clause 7 on page 3 of the Bill. The purpose of inserting the word " organization " in this clause was to give power to the commission to organize departments. The Senate moved to strike that out. As it is a

matter which in any event the commission would not be able to reach for a year or more, I think the amendment might be accepted. Another amendment is this. Under the Act as it stood in 1918, the Governor in Council had the power of appointing deputy ministers and members of Royal Commissions. By error this clause was deleted from the Bill, and this amendment is simply to restore the clause. There can be no objection whatever to the amendment.
Motion agreed to and Senate amendments concurred in.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

The administration will naturally fall to the departments that are particularly charged with carrying out the work to be done in accordance with the recommendations. For example, the Militia Department would1 naturally be concerned with gratuities; the rebate of transportation to dependents who returned to Canada prior to armistice would fall to the Immigration Department, which has been dealing with that problem-; while in regard to free clothing to patients in Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment hospitals, the department itself would take care of that work. The same is true of pay and allowances to trainees taken on the strength and afterwards not approved by that department. In regard to functional sub-normal cases, the committee recommend :
There is an urgent necessity for the establishing of a means to take care of these problem cases. In view of the highly technical and difficult nature of the question they recommend that the Department S. C. R. should take immediate steps to institute a thorough inquiry to determine the need and to recommend the means of best dealing with this difficult problem.
They further recommend that in the interim, or until such time as proper provision is made for the care of such cases, the department be authorized to expend the money necessary to make provision for these cases.
From the evidence that came before us, there is undoubtedly a large number of men1-we could not get anything .like .an estimate of the number- who have been discharged from the .army, who are not disabled in the ordinary sense, who are not being cared for by the department, and yet are sub-normal. I may give an example-of a man who came before us,' and I am sure there was not a member of the committee who did not feel that he should be in same institution. While he was not disabled in the ordinary sense, you could see written all over his face that he was certainly very sub-normal. He was out trying to get employment here, there and everywhere, and he struck us as being the type of man that must .be taken care of for some time in order to be brought back to normal mentality and strength. It was intimated to us that there were a good many cases of that kind throughout the country, and if this recommendation is carried out the department will have to. get in touch with them and wherever necessary make proper provision to take care of them. These men should not be .allowed to struggle for themselves for some months at least. If they are, I am afraid the consequences to them will be disastrous. It is exceedingly unfair that they should not be taken care of. As to what the expenditure will be, I am sure, as this committee can understand, it is very problematical. The committee has also recommended, and it seems to me that the House might very well leave it to the Government, that steps should be taken at once to ascertain what general policy should be.followed in regard to these men and what provision should be made to properly care for and treat them in order to bring them back, as far a.s po.ssible, to a normal condition. It seems to me that if the experts get to work at once and bring down recommendations as to the establishing of institutions or the placing of these men under proper care, or something of that kind, the Government should not delay in doing whatever is necessary. Again, recommendations were made in reference to certain classes of pension cases, more particularly of widows with families. It was felt that under existing conditions pensions did not go far enough. The committee felt that at this time they could not open up the whole pension system, and consequently made a general recommendation that provision should be made for necessitous cases until

the House has a further opportunity to consider the whole question of pensions. There was a further provision for the cashing of cheques of Canadians of the Imperial forces, in regard to which the expenditure will not he very large. Then' there were two concrete suggestions, one as to loans to re-trained disabled men for the tools and equipment which they require to establish themselves in a new line of work for which they are under training. This does not mean that they are to be established in business, but if they have been trained to be carpenters, blacksmiths, .shoemakers, or to engage in some other trade, a loan will be advanced to provide them with necessary tools. The other suggestion was for loans to disabled men for the purpose of training and education. It was represented that while certain men, such as university students or others who had been taking an educational course, might be getting a pension by reason of disability they had not the earning capacity to acquire what they needed in order to proceed with their education, and it was (Suggested that provision should be made .for loans in necessitous oases of this kind which would be considered on their merits. It is deemed advisable that loans should be given. There was a further suggestion in .regard to the probable unemployment situation during the coming winter. According to the evidence submitted to the committee, there are some 30,000 returned soldiers out of employment at the present time. We did not, of course, obtain, nor do I think it was possible to obtain, any evidence as to the proportion who were actually looking for employment, but the estimate of those not in employment was placed at 30,000. It was also estimated that anywhere from fifty to sixty or seventy thousand returned men would be out of employment during the winter, but it does not necessarily follow that all of these men will have to be provided for. All that the committee suggests is that necessitous cases of real hardship should be dealt with, every one being considered on its merits, and the necessary machinery established. The Government has not had time to consider what form that .administration will take, hut I can only repeat that I consider it very essential that whatever machinery is established should be established in .such .a way as to prevent this money being unnecessarily expended.

I desire to bring to the attention of the committee a matter that has reference particularly to

the territory I represent. It is referred to on page 34 of the report, Part VIII, Written Proposals Received, paragraph 2, and is embodied in a Memorial under date August 29, 1919, of the Yukon Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment Committee.
The memorial recites that quite a number of soldiers have returned to the Yukon and that the conditions affecting returned soldiers in the Yukon are as follows:
1.	That the Territory is essentially a mining
country.	.
2.	That the Territory during the war gave to its utmost both in men and money, almost to the breaking point.
3.	That the Territory received no benefit whatever from- war-time industrial activity; and that the Goverment Land Housing schemes are not possible of practical application here.
4.	That the Territory affords little employment during the winter months, and that many of the returned men have not sufficient funds to carry them through the winter.
5.	That the lays corporation of the Territory have considerable placer mining ground, which could be worked profitably .by "returned soldiers during the winter months, and there is other ground in the Territory that might be prospected during the winter months to advantage if the returned soldiers be given financial assistance.
Therefore 'be it resolved, that this committee prays that the necessary provisions be made at the forthcoming session of Parliament, whereby the sum of Thirty thousand dollars ($30.000) be appropriated for the benefit of Yukon returned soldiers, to assist them in becoming reestablished in their former occupation of mining, either in working ground on which discoveries have been made, or with a view of making new discoveries of gold and silver, in each case an agreement to be entered into with the returned soldiers, receiving assistance, whereby the amount so advanced by the Government shall he a first charge against the property he may acquire, or the mineral he may recover.
The committee believes that such a scheme will not only he beneficial to the community generally but will be the only solution of the problem of the unemployment of the returned soldiers in this Territory during, the coming winter.
That memorial was submitted to the committee of which my hon. friend (Mr. Calder) was chairman and it is recorded, as I have said, at page 34 of the report. In glancing over the report, however, I do not find that at has been specifically dealt with, and I would be glad if the minister would tell us as to whether he has been able in any degree to meet the wishes of the soldiers who have returned to the Yukon.

I have asked the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder), who was chairman of the committee which had this particular matter in hand, and who no doubt conducted that investigation with an ability equal to that shown by him in submitting the findings to the House, for a concise subdivision on this $40,000,000 which is to be voted to meet some of the recommendations in the committee so that I, and the committee, might know exactly what is to be done with the money. He has given a general outline of what is to be done. If I understand him aright there is nothing provided to meet any of the real demands that were made by the Great War Veterans' Association. They want some provision that would enable many returned soldiers to settle down and establish themselves in business. We have in the Land Settlement Act made very generous provision for the settlement of soldiers who are going on the land-expensive enough, dear knows, both to the country and to the soldier-and it is only to be hoped that it will be a success; if it is not it will be rather a bad thing for the soldier and an expensive experiment for the country. For the present let us hope that it will be a success and that the soldier, who is settled on the land will hawe no reason for complaint. I think he will have to admit that	he has been
generously dealt with.	But the large
body of men who are not inclined to settle on the land but are anxious to set-'tle down in other callings will realize that they are not so generously dealt with. The man who is disposed to be a farmer gets as high as $8,000. The Government has power to give that amount, and I think they have gone as high as that in some
cases. The man who wants to be a merchant, a tradesman, a fisherman, or perhaps a manufacturer, thinks that he should get the same consideration, or at least some consideration; and that was the basis of his application to the Government and to the committee, as I understand it. The opinion is that this concession should be made not so much by way of a donation or charitable assistance or anything of that kind. However, we have the report of the committee, and the only money that is provided is this $40,000,000 which is to be expended as the minister has just outlined. While this report is before the committee we studiously avoided talking in any way that would sound like politics or like seeking party advantage if party advantage could be gained. But as a representative of the people I am bound to tell the minister that I do not regard the investigation before the committee as absolutely fair. I do not regard it as fair in its inception, because the Government, of which the chairman is a distinguished member, had decided some time before July 27 last what they were going to do; that is they had decided that they were not going to do anything beyond those lines. That decision is found in a letter written by the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) 'on that day to the officials of the Great War Veterans' Association in Ottawa and addressed to iMr. MaoNeil who was, I believe, the secretary. The hon. minister (Mr. Calder) seems to indicate that he does not quite agree with this statement of mine.

These are but a few things which go to show that we might have been more conservative and looked farther ahead into the expenditure of money and have had to-day vastly larger money supplies in dealing with this very pressing question so that we could have held ourselves in a position to say to the soldier: We have the money, you need it, and if there is justification we will give it to you. Instead of that we are in the position of saying: you do need the money, and you are justified in looking for it, but we have not got the money to give. I submit, therefore, that this 140,000,000, while a very large sum of money, does not, according to the details given by the minister, in any way go to meet the demands that are made upon us by reason of the representations of the Great War Veterans' Association and the evidence which was submitted to the committee. However, we have nothing to do but to accept the conditions. Those conditions were accepted by a very large majority, the members of the House evidently indicating by their votes that they were perfectly satisfied with the provision that was thus being made for the
returned soldier. To me it was a disappointment.
Yesterday we had many hon. gentlemen speaking very strongly, eloquently and forcibly in support of something being done for the soldiers. I was sorry to see that there are evidently greater considerations than those which the .soldiers advanced; there are greater things than the needs of the returned soldier-things that are more influential in the matter of votes. The Minister of Immigration and Colonization has only to pull out his old musket and say: "Look here boys, there is one remedy for all these things'. If there is the slightest sign of weakness in our followers, we have a trick that will bring you to your milk-we shall resign." That flag was flown to the breeze, and every one faithfully filed up behind. Let the soldier look out for himself. ,.It was Safety First with hon. gentlemen on the other side.
I am very sorry that on account of the financial condition of the country, as found by this report, wre are not in a position to do better for our returned soldiers. I hope that the minister (Mr. Calder) will see to it that the very best administration is employed in disposing of this money as far as it goes. I have no doubt that he and his *colleagues will endeavour to the best of their ability to see that no money is wasted, and that the most pressing needs of the returned men are met as far as this little amount of money will meet them. With those observations to clear up exactly what my own views are on the subject, I have no objection at all to the passing of this item.
