I would like the hon. gentleman to take a little of his own treatment. I submit that in effect he said exactly what I have stated, and there is no other meaning to be taken from his words. But he forgot that there were members of that committee whom he had selected from his own side of the House, and who unanimously agreed with the other members of the committee that this report was the best they could recommend at this critical time in the history of the country. Yet the hon. leader,, of the Opposition stands up, for the purpose of cheap popularity, to try to make a point which recoils upon his own friend's with added force. Why, Mr. Chairman, with the number of discontented soldiers that apparently are to be found-though not to the same extent, I believe, as is generally thought^what would have been more popular for the committee to do than to have granted every reasonable demand of those soldiers? Popularity sought and popularity gained by going against one's honest convictions would be an infamous popularity. It is not right, I submit, for the hon. gentleman to say that the members of that committee entered upon their

work with a closed mind. On the contrary I assert that every member of -that committee-and every one of them is just as honourable as the hon. member who defames them-entered upon that inquiry with perfect honesty of purpose and with the intention of sifting to the bottom every just and reasonable claim put forward by those men who fought so valiantly for this country and the world at large, and that they entered upon the inquiry not with the knowledge imputed to them of the exact condition of the country's finances, but entered upon their task as men of probity and honour determined to do everything within the bounds of reason for the returned soldier. The hon. gentleman, in his very last sentence, condemns himself when he admits that he is very sorry, indeed, that the country's financial position would not allow the committee to do what he would have liked them to do. What is there in this parliamentary life that will enable the recognized leader of a once great party to defame members-honest men, men working with a set purpose to do their very best in their country's interests-and while defaming members on this side of the House to sully his own nest by heaping opprobrium upon those whom he himself appointed to the committee? speechtext:
Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 26 to amend the Canada Temperance Act. He said: Mr. Speaker, this Bill, as was explained when it was introduced, has for its purpose to enact a provision, applicable throughout the Dominion of Canada, in virtue whereof the importation- and, as the Bill was originally introduced, the manufacture also-of intoxicating liquor will be prohibited in the particular area designated, conditionally upon the majority of the Dominion electors in such areas voting for such prohibition. The area selected is the area of a province. The provinces are not dealt with nor referred to in this legislation in their quality of provinces having legislatures possessing separate and distinct legislative powers. I think it important to say this, because there seems to have been considerable misconception and misapprehension with regard to the effect of this legislation, and it has been referred to as legislation whereby this Parliament sought to confer or devolve upon provincial legislatures legislative powers belonging to this Dominion. I want to make it perfectly clear that the legislation has no such j>ur-

pose and will ha-ve no such effect. The legislation is Dominion-wide. Its substantial provision is that throughout this Dominion, wherever a majority of the people occupying the geographical area which constitutes any province vote in favour of prohibition of the importation of intoxicating liquor into that area, then in virtue of this Bill, legislation of the Parliament of Canada, prohibition of that importation shall come into force so far as that area is concerned.
The legislatures of the provinces are mentioned in the Bill only so far as they are designated as the bodies upon whose resolution the taking of the necessary plebiscite of the people occupying the area of any particular .province will be instituted under the provisions of this Bill. It does not purport to confer any legislative poiwe'r whatever upon the provincial legislatures. Their request is treated as sufficient to justify the setting in motion of the machinery provided by this Bill solely upon the ground tjiat it is assumed that the members composing any of those legislatures, being the representatives of the people occupying a provincial area, are in a position to know and express' what may be the desire of their constituents as regards simply the setting in motion of the machinery under this Bill. It raises no question of the powers of the legislature, nor can there properly arise under this Bill any question as to what are the powers of a provincial legislature.
Of course, this legislation can only stand if it be legislation upon a matter over which this Parliament has jurisdiction. The subject matter of this legislation is the importation in general of these intoxicating liquors, and, of course, included in that, the importation from the area of one province into the area of another. Certainly it cannot be suggested that provincial legislatures have any legislative authority over that question. I am confining myself to the question of importation, whether from outside of Canada or as between provinces, because, as I mentioned at the outset, though the Bill originally contemplated the prohibition either of manufacture or of importation or of both, the conclusion has been reached that we should amend-and I purpose when we go into 'Committee to move to amend-this Bill so as to>
make its provisions apply only to prohibition of importation. The reason for which I purpose to make that amendment is to he found in the legislation which was passed by this House this afternoon, and which I have no doubt will be passed by the Senate. That
legislation applies to the question of the manufacture of intoxicating liquor the rule laid down toy the Act passed1 by this House some years ago with regard to the importation of intoxicating liquor into a province, and so applying that rule, it prohibits the manufacture of intoxicating liquor for the purpose of being used in any way in violation of the law of any province. As a result of that legislation, without any plebiscite whatsoever we have in any province which prohibits the sale of intoxicating liquor prohibition of manufacture in that province of any liquor to be sold therein, and indeed to be sold in any other province where there is such prohibition of sale.
There is in addition to this amendment another amendment I purpose to make which is not without importance; that is to say, in order that a request emanating from the people of a province, transmitted through their legislative representatives, should be entitled to be acquiesced in by this Parliament, such request must come from a province which itself has already prohibited within its borders the sale of intoxicating liquor for beverage purposes. The reason why we have come to the conclusion that this provision should be introduced is, I think, obvious on a moment's reflection. There would certainly be no reason and no purpose in enabling the people occupying the area of a particular province to ask this House by a vote of their majority to prevent the importation into that province of intoxicating liquor if within that province the sale of intoxicatng liquor was permitted. Under these conditions, the effect of the prohibition would be simply to make a protection for the manufacturer and vendor within the limits of the province. That is certainly something that the Government would not ask this House to do; it is certainly something that I am sure the House would not be prepared to do no matter who asked them to do it.
I hope that I have made clear the purpose of this legislation. I hope I have made clear that we propose to restrict it to the question of importation, and that with regard to provincial areas in which the sale of liquor is prohibited. I emphasize also the fact that we do not by this legislation seek either to enlarge or to diminish-neither of which things could we do even if we tried

the legislative powers of provincial legislatures.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton and Victoria):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have
only one word to say to the minister (Hon. Mr. Doherty) about this Bill. I am afraid
1!W6

that if we divide up, so to speak, our customs laws into sections; if we have one class of customs laws in force in one province and another in another, considerable inconvenience will result and we shall not be able to effect the prohibition which the minister intends. If Nova Scotia complied with this Act and secured legislation prohibiting the importation of liquor into that province, and New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island had an open coast and open custom houses to receive liquors, it would be extremely difficult to keep liquor out of Nova Scotia. That illustrates the possible situation in all other parts of Canada. If Alberta passes a law prohibiting the importation of liquor into that province, and if at the same time liquor is allowed free access into British Columbia, it will be found very difficult to keep it out of the interior provinces. The genius of our customs laws is that they shall be universal; that they shall apply to the whole area of the country. Such a condition as I have indicated would make it exceedingly difficult to carry out the idea of temperance in provinces which take advantage of this legislation if other provinces choose to leave their coast open. I submit, therefore, that a prohibitory law, in order to be effective, must be universal.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's1):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would be very difficult, I am sure, to adopt any Bill in relation to the liquor traffic concerning which some astute lawyer could not raise grave doubts. The experience of the past is that no class of legislation is so productive of disputes as to the respective constitutional authorities of the Dominion Parliament and the local legislatures as legislation .affecting the liquor traffic. Into that aspect of the question I do not care to enter;' I take it for granted that the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Doherty) has taken a course *which, so far as his best ability and judgment goes, will stand the test of constitutional dispute. There is, however, one phase of this Bill to which, speaking for myself only, I take exception. I think that the proposal to require a plebiscite of the electors of any province is a grave mistake. This question of prohibition is part provincial and part Dominion. It is, provincial because the provinces have power to dio a great deal toward creating the prohibition, though they cannot, perhaps, use the word in its broad sense. On the other hand, there are some things which the provinces, cannot do-matters affecting importation, manufacture and the wholesale trade, which must

necessarily come, within the control of the Federal authorities.
In so far as my hon. friend is desirous of guarding against any invasion of provincial rights, I quite sympathize with his purpose. But it is a grave mistake to require the people of a given province to take a plebiscite on this question. My hon. friend says that the provincial legislatures ought to be capable of judging whether the people want something of this kind; therefore they are allowed!-to do what? Simply to ask that a plebiscite be taken. I think they are capable of doing more than that. If this legislation is to depend to any degree upon the action of any provincial authority it will be sufficient to let the legislature speak for the province. Let me give an illustration. There is no question that the people of Nova Scotia are in favour of prohibition. We have had, in one form or another, strong temperance legislation for many years. For a long time the Scott Act was in almost universal operation in that province; if I am not mistaken, there was a time when all jmt three counties were under the operation, of that Act. Then, in later years provincial legislation was enacted which seemed to be stronger than the Scott Act, and only for that reason the Scott Act was repealed in some counties. But to-day the legislature of Nova Scotia is strongly committed to prohibition; the province is unquestionably in favour of prohibition. Again, and again., in elections where the question has been raised, the people have given strong expression to that view. My own constituents, I am sure, require no plebiscite; their view is unmistakable; and so it is with the province at large. Why, then, should we ask the province to take a plebiscite? If the province is to have any say in the matter let the legislature of the province speak for the people, and let their voice prevail. This requirement to take ,a plebiscite will be a disappointment. Some provinces will not go to the trouble. It is an expensive thing; it isi a bother; it is a worry to the temperance people. I believe that the country will say that they ought not to he put to the expense and trouble and worry of a plebiscite. Whether the state of public opinion in the other provinces is as clearly indicated as it is in Nova Scotia, I cannot say, but I have already pointed out that a plebiscite would be quite unnecessary in my province. We have had plebiscites. We had a local plebiscite; we have had a Dominion, plebiscite; we have had legislation, Dominion and local; and to have the people of Nova

Scotia take another plebiscite on this question would certainly not be regarded as helping the camse of temperance. I strongly urge the minister, if he wants to take account of the views of the provinces-and I quite concur in his desire to do that-to accept the vote of the legislature of the province as the declaration of what t(he province wants and not put the people to the trouble of taking a plebiscite in a matter of this kind.

I cannot agree with the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding), although I am supporting this prohibition measure and the Government. A legislature or any other representative body must speak on the policy for which it was elected. For a legislature to go out of its way to make a request concerning .something which they were not instructed in by the people would simply be high-handed legislation and might lead to very' great trouble. As I say, I am supporting the Government in this, not because of any conviction that prohibition is right, because I think it is morally wrong. God is not a prohibitionist, and I propose to follow Him as long as possible.
I am speaking now simply to bring to your notice something that has been referred to, that bears very strongly upon the temperance sentiment of Ontario at least. -And that is something that was said by the Dominion Alliance to some of the members regarding this very legislation which is now contemplated. The Dominion Alliance has this to say about this legislation:
The measure now before Parliament will please no one, accomplish little or nothing; it will allow the reinstatement of the liquor traffic in Canada, and set province against province in a way that every true Canadian should strongly deprecate.
I hold no brief for the Dominion Alliance; but it is a very important body, and it strikes me that what it has to say in the matter should be well considered by those who are thinking of the matter.

Mr. Speaker, I am not unmindful of the danger one always runs in discussing in any public place, especially in the legislative halls of Canada, this question of temperance. No matter how remote the question may be, one is very apt to be blamed, whatever position one may take, by either one side or the other. It has been my intention since Bill No. 26 was read the first time in this House on October
7, to oppose the passage of that legislation through the House. The statement made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) on the motion to read the Bill the second time removed many of the objections that I had to the legislation. Perhaps the greatest objection to the Bill was removed when the minister stated that the Bill would not, in its original form, have any application to the manufacture of intoxicating liquors in any province for export. The Bill as it now comes before the House has been altered in many important respects, and now that it is confined simply to the importation of liquor into any province that has already declared its desire for prohibition, I shall confine the remarks I have to make to that branch of the Bill alone.
I regret th-at I find myself in a position where I feel obliged to oppose a measure of this kind, and in opposing it, I want to be clearly understood as not advocating the cause of the Liberty League or of any other association; nor, in fact, of the particular interests that are aimed at by this Bill, either at their request or by their influence or, so far as I know, with their knowledge. Nor do I desire, in opposing this Bill, to make any attack upon the interests of temperance in this Dominion or in this province, I rather approach the matter from a very much broader point of view. I do not think that the question of temperance is involved in this legislation except in a very general way. My objection to this legislation is based very largely upon the fact that it is in violation of the constitution of this Dominion. I know that the Minister of Justice has made a statement to the contrary, but lawyers all differ.
Even judges.

And courts of law, as well. Notwithstanding the opinion advanced by the Minister of Justice, I would invite the attention of the House to section 121 of the British North America Act, upon which I rely in making this statement, and which reads:
All articles of the growth, produce, or manufacture of any one of the provinces shall, from and after the union, he admitted free into each of the other provinces.
Any article, therefore, that is the manufacture of one province shall, according to the clause of the constitution that I have just read, be admitted free into another province.
Does that not mean " free of duty?"

I do not take it so. If that had been the object of the constitution, it would have said so. The clause to which I have referred says that it shall be admitted free, without any qualification whatever, and I take it that the clause of the constitution which I have read means exactly what I have said. If that be the meaning of the clause, then I say that it is not within the jurisdiction of
10 p.m. this Parliament to impose any restriction upon any one province in regard to its sending any article of its manufacture into another province or receiving any article manufactured by another province. Intoxicating liquor is a manufactured product in the province of Ontario, in which there are some seven or eight very large distilleries manufacturing that product, and after the passage of this Bill, they will continue to manufacture it at least for export. By this legislation it is pro' posed to prohibit the importation of that manufactured product into, say the province of Quebec or any other province that may pass prohibitory legislation, and I do not believe it to be within the jurisdiction of this Parliament to do that. A case very similar to the point raised here has already been tried and determined by the Appellate Court, the highest court in the Commonwealth of Australia, in whose constitution a similar provision is made, admitting the product of one state of the Commonwealth into another either by sea or land traffic.
Legislation was passed fixing a different fee for the vending of wine in one state from that ifor the sale of similar wine manufactured in another state of the Commonwealth. That case was carried to the highest court of the Commonwealth. It was held that there was no jurisdiction in the State to pass such legislation, and the judgment of the magistrate in the first instance dismissing the case was upheld by the unanimous decision of the court. That, I may say, is the only direct case in point which I have been able to discover, but it seems to me to be so analogous to the case in hand that it would be very dangerous in the face of that, and in the face of the ordinary reading of the clause, to proceed with legislation of this kind. It is bound, it appears to me, to provoke a very great deal of litigation in any event. If the Bill were passed with that clause in it restricting the importation, I doubt not that interested parties would take up the question and it would be subject to

litigation probably for a very long time and with very considerable expense.
In addition to this, I take the further ground that, inasmuch as power is vested in this Parliament alone to legislate in regard to the question of importation, that power cannot be delegated to any other legislative body in the Dominion. In his remarks the Minister of Justice stated that the passing of this proposed legislation would not transfer the authority to the Provincial Governments. I cannot understand that statement in view of the effect which it is endeavouring to accomplish by this legislation. As matters stand now, any legislature in the Dominion has the right to apply by petition or resolution to this Parliament to pass enabling legislation just the same as would have to be passed after a referendum'had been taken under this Act. No legislature in Canada requires such legislation as this to give it power to come and ask Parliament for enabling legislation, and I argue therefore that there is no necessity for this measure. It does not accomplish v_any purpose. But even if it does, what does it do? As conditions are now, upon a petition or resolution being presented to this House by a Provincial Government, this House, dn its wisdom, can say "yes" or "no". But if it is passed, this Act declares that upon a referendum being taken and a majority voting in favour of prohibition, then that prohibition shall come into force by Order in Council. While this Parliament will be the legislature in which enabling legislation will finally have to be passed, yet by the passing of this Bill it puts itself in the position in which it cannot say " no"; it must say " yes ". Its position now enables it to say either "yes" or "no.", as Parliament may deem wisest and best. Now, legislation that has that effect of taking the power out of the hands of this Parliament and, if I may use the expression to emphasize my point if possible, tying it hand and foot so that it can give only one answer, is tantamount to handing over to the province that may submit a resolution to Parliament the power to compel this body to act in a certain way. If that is nob ^delegating the authority of this Parliament it is at least curtailing it to such an extent that Parliament cannot deny any application that may be made in a matter of this kind.
For these two reasons upon the legal aspect of the matter, Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to the further progress of the Bill through the House. Even if this proposed

legislation is within the province of Parliament, again I say I do not think it desirable. I do not think that it is wise for this Parliament to proceed with it, for a number of reasons which I shall endeavour to enumerate. I recognize, and I trust the Government recognizes, with the example that we had only a few short days ago, that, from the amount of sympathy any legislative body receives from any province-or from a certain province, I may say-for passing prohibitory legislation, experience teaches that such legislation does not meet with gratitude on the part of those in whose favour it is enacted; and also teaches the lesson that it is treated in a spirit of revenge by those against whom it operates. And while I do not wish to prophesy, if I were asked for an opinion upon the question, I would say that this Government would probably receive similar treatment, as a result of a similar action to that taken by the legislature of Ontario.
My first objection, therefore, to the further progress of this legislation, apart from the legal aspect, is that no one is asking for it. So far as I have been able to discover, there is not a province in the Dominion of Canada that has asked for this legislation. The temperance people-if I read correctly the extracts from the paper of the Dominion Alliance- do. not want it, and as the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) said, they have condemned this legislation as not accomplishing any purpose in the interests of temperance.
I am satisfied that those who are opposed to prohibition are not asking for this legislation. No one seems to be asking for it. Everybody seems to be opposing it, speaking for these two bodies, and yet the Government thinks it wise, with the history that I have already referred to before them, to press this legislation upon the House.
I take further objection that legislation such as this, so drastic in its nature, should not be pressed or passed by any Government without a direct mandate from the people asking that it be done. There is no mandate from the people for legislation of this kind. It is a very good rule to be observed in Parliament as well as in private life to wait until such time as one is asked for -a favour of this kind before granting it. It appears to me that by passing a measure of this kind the Government is handing out to the people of Canada something that they have not asked for and something that they have declared against.
The same object can be accomplished by any of the provinces desiring it without the aid of this legislation as can be accomplished by it. This legislation, from what I have been able to glean from members of the Cabinet and others, seems to be anticipating trouble in the future in regard to the question of temperance and to be an endeavour to shift the responsibility of this Parliament upon the shoulders of some other Parliament in order to avoid that trouble. If, as I have stated, under the British North America Act, power is granted exclusively to this Parliament to legislate in regard to total prohibition of importat-tion of intoxicating liquors, it is the duty of this Parliament to preserve that power. We have a duty to perform in exercising that power and I hope that we will, as men, when the question comes before this House, take the full responsibility that rests upon us, having that power and having that duty to perform. I do not believe it is fair to the members of this House or to members of the legislatures that any attempt should be made to shift the responsibility of this Parliament upon the shoulders of some other legislature. Whatever duty we have to perform we should perform without fear, and whatever responsibility is attached to that we should be willing to bear. For that reason, I for one am opposed to any endeavour to shift that responsibility or to give that power to any legislative body. I * am quite ready and prepared when the question comes before this House, if it ever should come before this House while I am in it, to take my share of responsibility in saying whether prohibitory legislation should be passed in regard to this great question or not. I think every hon. member of this House should be prepared to treat it in the same way.
There is in the province of Ontario a very large interest represented by the distillers. As I stated in my opening remarks,
I have no interest particularly in them; I am not speaking on their behalf at all; but there is a very large interest in the seven or eight distilleries in that province. There is one very close to my own riding in which millions of dollars are invested. The business affords a good market-asplendid market-for the products of the farm not only in, grain, but. in the hay and cattle that are raised upon the farm and that are consumed at these distilleries. They offer a good market for the products of the farm. They contribute a very large amount of revenue to the Government of this country.
Mr. McMAS'TER: What is the hay used for?

For feeding the cattle. They buy large numbers of cattle, feed them upon the refuse from the distilleries, and they buy hay to supplement that feed. The distilleries also provide a large amount of revenue for the particular municipalities in which they are situated. What this legislation means is in a very large measure the destruction of these industries. It will affect them most seriously. But I would not argue that for one moment as a reason why this legislation should not be passed if I were convinced that such legislation was in the interest of the people of Canada as a whole or that the people desired it. Until it is demonstrated to this Parliament that the people are asking for legislation of this character I think it would be well for Parliament to hold its hand and not force upon the people something that they have riot asked for but that they have, in the way I have already spoken of, condemned.
Another objection I raise to this legislation is that the precedent set in transferring or delegating the power- of this Parliament to some other legislative body is a most dangerous one. The power of this Parliament-during, the twenty years, or nearly twenty years, that I have been in it-is one of the things*, I might say the principal thing, that Parliament has been molt jealous of in guarding and protecting; and if Parliament once gives way to the delegation of its power to any other legislative body I think what may reasonably be expected is that those other legislative bodies will be hereafter continually endeavouring to encroach upon the power of the federal authority and seeking to acquire as much of that power as it might be possible for them to do. It is a dangerous precedent to set. It seems to me this Parliament should retain the power in its own hands, fulfil its own duties, and bear its own responsibilities. This legislation, even prohibiting the importation alone, is a discrimination. It is legislation in the way of discrimination in favour of one province against another. Did the same condition prevail in all the provinces of Canada, then one could understand such legislation being applied; but where there is a different condition existing in a very great number of the provinces, and when this legislation says that although liquor may be imported in one province it cannot be taken into another, or that people living in another province cannot avail themselves of a Canadian product manufactured at their own door, or next door to them, but that they must send the money-

if they are bound to have intoxicating liquor-to some foreign country, and import into a wet province, we will say, any amount of liquor they may desire, it seems to me that is bad legislation in the way of discouraging the manufacture at home and discriminating in favour of one province as against another. -
Does the hon. gentleman take into consideration the fact that this Government, through the Canada Temperance Act, delegates to the counties the right to enact restrictive legislation?

That may be so, but the fact that it did so on one occasion does not justify it in doing a wrong a second time.
Mr. J. E. ARMiSTRONG: What is the difference between giving that power to a county and extending it to a province?

I say the principle is the same; it is vicious in' both instances and should not be given at all. I had intended, Mr. Speaker, making a motion in regard to this matter, but as I think the same object can be attained when the Bill goes into Committee of the Whole-if it does go-I shall not make the motion now, but will reserve what further remarks I have to offer in that regard until the Bill reaches that stage.
Turning to the Bill itself, it seems to me that it would be impossible, if the measure goes through in the form in which it is now presented, in the event of a referendum being carried by a prohibitive majority vote, that that legislation could ever be enforced.
I think it is a well-known and' recognized fact that in regard to legislation of this character there must be a strong body of public opinion behind it, in order that it may be properly and effectively enforced. Now, by the provisions of this Bill, a majority of a single vote would be all that would be required to compel this Parliament to say that this legislation .shall go info effect. I do not believe that such legislation is wise legislation.
Then, pointing out what I conceive to be another defect in the Bill, let me say that under the provisions of this Act a province, by simply passing a resolution, may come to this- House and demand a referendum. All the expense of providing the machinery for that referendum-of preparing the voters' lists and everything in connection with it

 must be borne by this Parliament.
They do not come to this House; they go to the Governor in Council.

Yes, they go to the Governor in Council. That expense, as I say, must all be borne by the Federal Parliament. Now, I cannot see the justice of imposing that obligation upon the Federal Government, whose revenue is contributed to by every province in the Dominion, and to compel every such province to contribute its part towards passing prohibitory legislation in any one province. It occurs to me that it would be much fairer, and it would be just, if a province seeking legislation of this kind were required to hold the referendum itself and to undertake all the expense and trouble connected therewith; and after that referendum had been held-if such a thing is necessary at all, and I argue that it is not-then to come to this Parliament, [DOT]and, having paid its own expenses, paid its [DOT]own way, ask for the enabling legislation. It seems to me that that would be the fair thing to do.
Another feature of this Bill that does not commend itself to me is this: The amended Bill, or the measure that is now before the House, contains a provision which the original Bill did not contain-that a vote for the passing of such enabling legislation shall not occur oftener than every three years. Follow that out to its logical conclusion. Take the several provinces in the Dominion. The province of Ontario comes to this Parliament, we will say, at its next session, with a resolution which says: " Hold a referendum and pass this legislation." The Federal Government is in the position then that it must support that referendum, and, if it is carried, pass the necessary legislation or Order in Council to give effect to the wishes of the province. The very next year, the province of Quebec may come along with another resolution, and the same thing has to be gone through with again and the same expense incurred. Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia, or any of the other provinces may be coming along, one session after another, and -we will have the spectacle of a referendum going on in this country, probably for the next eight or ten years, before all the provinces will have been dealt with, and by the itime the whole body is -served under this Act the three years prescribed in the case of the first province will have expired and it will foe coming back again-that is, supposing the referendum to have been defeated. That is not a desirable position and yet it seems to me it is the logical and real position in which -we will be placed by such legislation as is proposed here.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I desire to say that this legislation will have the effect that I have already stated of transferring or delegating the power of this Parliament to another legislative body, or it is hypocritical. It professes to make such a transfer; but if there is something in the Bill that I have not fully appreciated and that still leaves a card up the sleeve of the Government by which they may defeat that purpose, why, I have not discovered it. I believe this legislation constitutes a transfer of power from this Parliament to another legislative body. If it does not do that, then I say it does not do what it professes to do. Furthermore, if this Bill does not grant absolute power to a province to force such legislation, then it is hypocritical in regard to the temperance people, because it purports to give them something which in reality it does not give them. For these various reasons, Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to the further passage of this Bill.
Mr. .T. E. ARMSTRONG (East Lambton): Mr. Speaker, the member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter) appears to be exercised over curtailing the powers of this Parliament, but he must admit that since 1878 the Canada Temperance Act has been in force and that the expense connected with the carrying out of that Act has been borne by this Parliament, no matter where that expense has been incurred. I am sure that the present legislation is merely extending that principle one step further so that the provinces may be assisted in bringing about legislation which they believe is in their interests to have enacted.
The member for West Hastings calls attention to the fact that we have not a mandate to carry out this legislation. But we are merely providing means, as I understand it, whereby a mandate can be given in the different provinces.
It is generally understood that on Tuesday next peace will be officially declared, Mr. Speaker, and after that date we expect that the Order in Council which has been in force for the past few years governing the importation, manufacture and sale of liquor in the different provinces will become inoperative. Consequently it is the duty of this Parliameirt to provide legislation similar to the legislation which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) has now brought forward in order that those provinces	which intend	to	bring about
prohibition of the liquor traffic within their boundaries may be in a position to do so. This Bill provides all the necessary

machinery to effect that. The Federal Government will be compelled to accept a resolution passed by any provincial legislature and to submit a referendum, and if the people volte in favour of total prohibition it will he the duty of this Parliament to prohibit the importation of liquor into that particular province.
It i.s not my intention to take up any more of the time of the House, but I have an amendment which I would like to submit in connection with this Bill, which is seconded by the hon member for Macdonald (Mr Hendexs) and reads as follows:
That clause 152- of Bill No. 26, an Act to amend the Canada Temperance Act, be amended by adding at the end thereof paragraph (a), which reads as follows-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member knows that he would in any event not be in a position ito move that amendment at this stage. It will be quite proper for him to do so when the Bill is in committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the hon. member (Mr. Doherty) desire to reply?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Minister of Justice is closing the debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course, I do not want to cut off debate, but I feel it would be less than courteous on my part not to make answer to the very interesting observations that we have heard on this Bill. With regard to the remarks of the leader of the Opposition as to the disadvantages of having what he describes as a customs law not * applicable to the entire country, while I cannot look upon this measure as a customs law, I quite concur in the proposition that, of course, if importation were absolutely prohibited into any part of the Dominion it would be more certain that intoxicating liquor would not get into any particular province. But we are not dealing, with anything in the nature of a customs law. The purpose of this Bill, as I pointed out, is to enable such provinces as desire that their own provisions prohibiting the sale of liquor within their areas should be strengthened and fortified by the prohibition of importation of liquor into their midst, and having that in mind, and proceeding upon the principle that in the

matter of a law of this nature it is highly important that it should be enacted to be operative only in a province where public opinion will stand behind it and make it susceptible of real enforcement, we necessarily reach the result that, if different provinces should be of 'a different opinion as to whether liquor should come into their midst or not, we have to face the difficulty which the hon. gentleman suggests.
The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) said that he recognized the difficulties or the dangers of litigation probably arising with regard to any legislation dealing with the prohibition question. I think that the address we have had from the hon. member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter) has quite justified the statement of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's. But of course, if we are going to deal with the subject of prohibition, we have to face the fact that questions may be raised as to the constitutionality of our legislation.	*
I have given to the question the best consideration of which I am capable, and I have had the valuable assistance of other legal members of the Government and of the law officers of the Crown. It appeared to us that we kept within the limits prescribed to us by the constitution in drafting this legislation.
The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) etxpressed the view that instead of resorting to a plebiscite it would be more desirable to let the Legislature of the province determine this question, and upon its authority have importation prohibited. If that were possible constitutionally, I quite recognize that there would be advantages in that course. But an attempt to do that, would, I think, not only give rise to constitutional questions-, but might enable such questions to be successfully raised and our legislation to be declared unconstitutional. The hon. member for West Hastings (Mr. Potter) has made an argument which demonstrates that proposition. It is not in our power to delegate to a Provincial Legislature power to enact a measure upon a matter which, under the British North America Act, is not within its legislative jurisdiction.
I did not suggest that the Legislature should be given any such power. My point was that a petition from the Legislature was just as effective as a petition by way of plebiscite.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, the petition under this legislation does come from the Pro-

vincial Legislature. The Act provides that upon the resolution- or petition of the Legislature we shall set the machinery in motion.
In neither case would there be an enactment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, but even though that petition had not the form of an enactment, we would, by providing that the petition should bring our law into force, proceed to enact legislation immediately effective to govern the people of this country, at the option of a Provincial Legislature. It would only be an indirect manner of submitting the existence and force of our laws to the action of a Legislature.

Do I understand the minister to argue that under this legislation the provinces will not have the right to come to this Parliament or to the Governor in Council and demand certain legislation? In other words, this Parliament cannot say a thing once a Legislature takes certain action. Is that not a power on the part of the province to force this Parliament to legislate in a certain manner?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is what Parliament is saying toy this Bill: We think that a resolution adopted by a provincial legislature is a sufficient expression of opinion on behalf of the people of the province in ques-tkn to justify this Parliament in conferring upon the Governor in Council the power to enable the people of that province to express th-eir views upon the question. The action of the legislature in that case merely takes the place of the twenty-five per cent oLthe electors who must petition under the -Scott Act; and that provision is made simply for the sake of convenient and practical operation. It would be imposing a very onerous condition to ask that twenty-five per cent of the electors of a province join in a petition. On the other hand, it might be said that to accept the petition of a smaller percentage would be accepting a petition not representative of the general opinion of the country. It is true that the members of a legislature are elected to perform certain functions, and we cannot and do not pretend to confer upon them any additional power to legislate with regard to their province. But they are representative of the whole body of the people, and this Parliament points them out, so to speak, as a body sufficiently representative of the people of the province to- justify the Governor in -Council in accepting their intimation that a plebiscite would be desirable as expressing the general view of those people.
Can the same result not be obtained without this legislation at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What result?

Can the results sought to be obtained by this Act not be obtained by the provincial Parliament petitioning this Government for enabling legislation? This Government could then deal with the matter without this legislation -at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Frankly, I do not understand my hon. friend's reference to passing legislation to enable legislatures to do things. The Order in Council which will be passed under this law can in no way be described as legislation enabling a legislature to do something . The proclamation that will issue will go directly to the people; it will have nothing to do with the legislature. The hon. gentleman ought to remember that, while all of us form part of the people of some province, we also form part of the people of the whole of Canada, and this is legislation for the whole of Canada. If a majority of the people in each of the areas that constitute the geographical area of a province say: We do not want liquor to come into our community, then under the law of the Parliament of Canada, without the slightest legislative intervention of any legislature, that prohibition will come into effect.
It is local option.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is- local option, with the area enlarged. Could it be said that the provision of the Scott Act that the sale of liquor should toe prohibited in counties where the majority of the people said they did not want liquor sold was a delegation of legislative power to that county or that county council? The question whether legislation of this kind involves a delegation of power was threshed out in the case of Russell and the Queen. There precisely the arguments that are, now -being made were urged; that Parliament was delegating its power and that Parliament could not delegate its power. Well, I abundantly agree that Parliament cannot delegate its power.
But it was there held that it was no delegation of power on the part of Parliament to enact provisions of law on its own authority, as the Scott Act does and as we are doing, and to make the condition of those provisions becoming operative in particular sections that the majority of the people should express their desire that they should become operative. The legislation is absolutely sound; it is law throughout the Dom-

inion; but the condition of its operation in a particular area is that the majority of the people in that area should say that they desire it. To meet what may be a very desirable end of having a legislature deal with this, we would have to do the impossible thing of delegating our powers to the legislature, and I quite agree that the hon. member for West Hastings has demonstrated the unconstitutionality of any endeavour to do that. But in reply to him I would say. as I said at the outset and as I will try to make clear now, that we are not delegating powers of this Parliament at all. The legislature as a legislative body plays no role here; nothing that it does here makes law; but this Parliament, if it enacts this legislation, decides that in its opinion, if that body of men who are elected for certain purposes by the people occupying the area of a province, express to the Government of this country the view that .those people desire a plebiscite, then the Government of this country may and shall-

They can compel the
Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They can have no mandamus to do it; but it will be the clear duty of the Government to issue the proclamation ordering the plebiscite. Why? Because this Parliament has said to the Government: That is sufficient evidence to justify you in doing it, and this Parliament tells the Government to do it. It is not the province that is making the Government take this action; it is this Parliament that by its enactment says: Upon such action by that gathering, we tell you that it is a proper thing to order a plebiscite; and when the Government comes to do that it will not be because the legislature of a province has made the Government do it, it will be because this Parliament said that under those circumstances the Government ouglht to do it. The Government will be doing it as the executive of this Parliament, carrying out the will of this Parliament. There seems to me to be in the minds of many people a confusion which appears to result from this that, whenever you mention a province, you are necessarily mentioning it as an entity entitled to have a legislature of its own, sovereignty to legislate about certain particular subjects. No doubt if you are reading the British North America Act and concerned with questions of distribution of legislative powers, that is what the problem is. But the area of the province of Ontario, or of the province of Quebec, or of the province of British Columbia, is part of the area of Canada;

the people of each one of those provinces form part of the people of Canada; and this is legislation by the Parliament of the whole of Canada on a .subject,
11 p.m. that is, the subject of interprovincial importation of any liquor and importation from the outside also- because this prohibition, if it comes into force, does not merely prohibit taking from one province into another but will just as effectively prohibit importation from outside into that province. I mention that because of one of the arguments brought forward by the hon. member (Mr. Porter).
It seems to me that, because we choose to designate the area within which the population, whereof may, by a majority, determine that it wants this as coterminus with the area of a province, it does not necessarily follow that we are in any way concerned with the powers of the legislature of that province which could not under any circumstances make any laws about this interprovincial traffic or about the importation of liquor. It can be no more said that we are affecting the powers of the legislature than that the .Scott Act affects or touches, increases or diminishes, the power of the county council of the county which passes the Scott Act.
The hon. member for West Hastings referred to section 121 of the British North America Act, which section declares that all the produce or manufacture of each province must pass free into every other province, and he argued from that that there was no power anywhere, I should take it, without amendment of the. British North America Act, to interfere with the passage of the produce or manufacture of one province into another. In the first place, you have the use of the word " free ", and that on its face indicates that what the legislation was thinking of at the time was the imposition of anything in the nature of duties or restrictions of a fiscal nature upon products. That is confirmed by the fact that the particular section forms part of a number of sections dealing with fiscal questions. We had occasion to .go very carefully into that question when we originally passed the Act which we amended this afternoon, the Act which has a very long title and which people, in order to avoid that long title, have come to oall the "Doherty Act." Section 121 of the British North America Act, which contains the word " free," forms part of subdivision 8, and the title of this subdivision is "revenues; debts; assets; taxation." If in a portion of the British

North America Act dealing with taxation, you find the provision that goods, the manufacture of one province, must be admitted into another free, it seems to me that it is an undue extension to extend that to mean, as the hon. member's interpretation would, that if the most noxious thing that one could conceive, the most absolutely deadly poison, were manufactured in one province of this Dominion, it would be beyond the power of this Parliament to say: It shall not pass outside of that province into another. 'The article is looking at the subject from the point of view indicated in the general title, and the general title, with the use of the word " free," puts the matter beyond doubt. While I say that, I say it with all respect to the hon. gentleman, who himself points out that lawyers sometimes differ. I am going to agree to that, and ll do not put down my opinion in any dogmatic way. But it is the opinion which I entertain very strongly, and I feel that if this is good legislation there is no ground for hesitation in passing it because of that particular article.
The hbn. gentleman referred to an Australian case. I am not familiar with it, nor with the provisions of the constitution of the Australian 'Commonwealth.
But on the very face of the case as he explained it to us, that was a question as to whether one state within the Commonwealth had a right to differentiate between the amount of fee that it would imipose upon goods manufactured in another state, and that which it would impose on goods manufactured -within itself. Well, just so soon as any one of our provinces says it will put on a tax on certain things manufactured in the next province which it will not impose on things manufactured within itself, then you will have a case analogous to the one cited and there will no doubt be a judgment similar to that one. The hon. gentleman sipoke of Parliament's hands being tied and having no possibility of saying "no" when the petition comes. Parliament will not have anything to say in any*event on the subject. The petition or request will go to the Governor in Council, and the Governor in Council will say "yes," because this Parliament has told it to say "yes"

not because the province is compelling Parliament to accept its petition.
The hon. gentleman made some reference to the fate that befell people who enacted legislation on provincial lines. Well, I would be sorry to take as lugubrious a view as he does as regards the consequences. But after all that is not the question before
us. The question before us is: Is this good legislation? If it is we ought to pass it even if we pass on to our own political funeral. The hon. gentleman also protested against an endeavour to shift our responsibilities upon other legislative bodies. Having, as I hope, made it clear that we are not delegating our powers to any legislature, I think it is equally clear that we are shifting no responsibilities upon any one. We here to-night are taking the full, entire and complete responsibility of enacting a law which recognizes that-if a majority of the people of a province do not want liquor in their midst from outside they need not have it. And for my part I am sure that all of us will have no hesitation in assuming the responsibility of determining that question one way or the other. There is no shifting of responsibility. This is a question upon which the will of the people themselves should he allowed to be exercised. The people living in the different areas that constitute the provinces should have the right-I was going to say the privileges, but it is better to describe it as a right-to say for themselves whether liquor should go in among them or not.
Where does the minister connect the people he is speaking of now with the provincial legislature?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not connect them in the remotest degree.
How does the minister connect the people of that provincial area he is speaking of with the body which, for convenience, we call the provincial legislature?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: So far as the operation of this law is concerned I do not connect them at all. I deal with them as Canadian people. It is the Dominion electors who are going to vote on this question, and it is in their capacity as Dominion electors that they will do so; and if the legislature express the opinion that the people of a province desire a plebiscite, then I ask \hat Parliament shall justify the Government in accepting that as sufficiently representative of the desire on the part of the people of the province to have a plebiscite. It would be quite competent for any legislature to express its opinion as to whether it would he desirable that a law which it cannot enact should be enacted by the body that has legislative power to do it. When the legislature expresses that opinion, Parliament says to its executive: You will be justified in 'allowing the people
But this Parliament would be depriving itself of its power to say " yes" or " no."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Every time this Parliament enacts a law it deprives itself of the power of saying anything to the contrary until it chooses to repeal that law. And after this Parliament passes>
this law, if it ever changes its mind and wants " no ", it will have nothing in the world to do but to repeal the Act.
The hon. gentleman referred to difficulties regarding injustice to manufacturers. I have pointed out that we have dropped the manufacturing question entirely, and their cattle can go on being fed on the various things that arise out of the benefits of having distilleries, so far as this Act is concerned. He also spoke of this as a discrimination against a manufacturer in an adjoining province in favour of the outsider. I have already pointed out that prohibition on importation from one province to another will also prohibit importation into that province from outside of Canada.
There is an objection on the ground of expense. Now, this is Dominion legislation. The people who vote on these plebiscites will be exercising a right conferred by the Parliament of Canada, a right which no other body but this Parliament could confer, and this legislation is being enacted, as it should be enacted, because it is good legislation for the Dominion. It is good that in the Dominion the people should have an opportunity of expressing their will upon this subject, and having that will respected. That being so, on what ground could we ask the province, which cannot legislate on the matter, to pay the expenses in connection with the exercise by citizens of Canada of a right conferred upon them by the Parliament of Canada, because that Parliament believes that it is good for the people of the different provinces to exercise that right.
I have tried, Mr. Speaker, to the best of my ability, to reply to the observations that have been made on the subject, and I have done so with no desire to be dogmatic but to give my reasons why condemnation of this Bill is not justified.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the second time.
On motion of Hon. Mr. Doherty the House went into committee on the Bill, Mr. Steele in the Chair.

On section 1 of the Bill, covering section 152 as proposed to be added to the Canada Temperance Act, subsection 1-Upon receipt of resolution of Legislative Assembly or of Yukon Council requesting vote on prohibition or importation of liquors, the Governor in Council may issue proclamation.

I should like to draw
attention to a point dealt with by the hon. member for West Hastings, and also by the Minister of Justice. I want to say however, that I quite agree with the Minister of Justice that the only body which proposes to legislate on this matter at the present time is the Parliament of Canada. When I say " legislate " I mean passing a law. A resolution is not legislation. I quite agree with that view. But what strikes me as remarkable is the distinction that the minister has drawn between the legal effect of a petition from the provincial legislature and a petition from the people. My suggestion was that if it was deemed desirable to have an exnression from the provincial authority the legislature itself should be the authority to express that opinion instead of securing that expression through a plebiscite. The Minister of Justice concurs in my view that it would be very desirable, but he says that if we allowed the legislature to make that request we would be delegating our power.
It is only on that point that I want to say a few words. I respectfully submit that there is no question of delegation in one ease or the other; in both cases it is simply a petition, there is no actual legislation. In the case I suggest the legislature might pass a resolution or petition asking the Dominion Government to enact this law or to carry out the provisions of a law already enacted. In another case a resolution of the legislature is passed to be followed by a plebiscite. In both cases it is simply a petition. In the one case it is the petition of the legislature and in the other it is the petition of the people, but in neither case is it a legislative enactnfent. In neither case can it be deemed a delegation.

Might I ask the hon.
gentleman if he is not, in that case, substituting the opinion of a small body of men for the opinion of the whole people?

Quite so, but that does not affect my point. It will not affect the constitutional position. My point is that neither in one case nor in the other is there

any delegation, or anything more than a mere petition, and, as respects the constitutional position, whether that petition comes from the legislature, or in the form of a plebiscite, it is precisely the same thing. If it is proper to accept the result of a plebiscite, it would be proper to accept the judgment of the Legislature of the province. That is my contention. I can see no possible difference between the two. The Minister of Justice says that all we would do would be to substitute the legislature for the twenty-five electors under the Canada Temperance Act. Is the legislature the body to be substituted for that purpose? If that is all we want why not take the executive council? That is a representative body. The legislature is not twenty-five electors; the legislature represents the whole of the electors and if you only want something to substitute for the twenty-five, why not take the executive council? But the main point I desire to make is this: We have had plebiscites enough on this question. The hon. member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter) is quite correct when he says that nobody wants this Bill. Certainly the temperance people do not want it and speaking from the point of view of my own province, I am sure the proposal for another plebiscite will not be viewed with favour. If it be deemed necessary to get an expression of opinion from the province it would be much better and much more satisfactory to everybody to accept a resolution from the provincial legislature rather than to take a plebiscite.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would like to point
out what to my mind is the distinction between what the hon. gentleman suggests, namely, that we should legislate and that upon the request of the legislature this law should operate-<-
We will already have legislated, and we will only have to bring the law into effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The suggestion is that
the Act bringing it into effect should be dependent upon the legislature's request.
True.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The distinction between that and our making it dependent upon the vote of the people themselves is that if we now enact the law and say that it shall be operative within the province if the legislature ask for it, we in effect confer upon the legislature by an Act of its own as a legislature the power to impose upon the people of the province the law that we have
enacted. If we pass the legislation in that way it will be the action of the legislature that will subject the people of the province to this law. That in whatever form it takes, is in substance putting into the hands of the legislature the power of determining whether the people of the province shall or shall not be subject to this law that the Dominion Parliament has enacted. While we in form will be enacting the law, the decision that will subject the people of the province to it will he the decision of their legislature. Now, that legislature has no power to subject the people of their province to the operation of any law unless it is a law the subject matter whereof comes within the provisions of section 92 of the British North America Act, and this subject of importation does not.
That, whether it is sufficient or not, is a reason why, to my mind, the concrete action suggested by the hon. gentleman would make our legislation unconstitutional. Proceeding as we do, no man in any province of Canada becomes subject to this law by reason of the decision of any other legislative body. We are merely making an expression of the people a condition of our law becoming operative.

We have heard it said repeatedly that the Government is not by this action expressing the will of the people. Take a hypothetical case where the Government or the Legislative Assembly might be hostile to prohibitory legislation; they might be thwarting the will of the people. The people themselves might be in a large majority and wish this step to be taken but the Government or the legislature [DOT] might refuse to take the step. Would there be any remedy at the hands of the people if that condition arose?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It would not be the Provincial Government that would have to take the step; it would he the legislature. The remedy that would be in the hands of the people in that event would be to elect another legislature.
That takes time; it means four or five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is true. If the legislators of the province do not do what the electors would like to have done, it is inherent in our constitution that the electors must wait for the remedy which is to substitute new representatives.
Mr, E, LAPOINTE:	The same thing for
thi^ Parliament,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The same thing for this Parliament. I can understand that there may be that objection but we must find some method by which the request can he met. Now if we impose the requirement we must have a petition that in some way will be representative of some volume of opinion in the province. If we impose the necessity of 25 per cent of the electors of a province signing that petition we would be imposing a most onerous condition upon the portion of the population that may desire to have the plebiscite. It was from that point of view that we thought we could not follow out the idea of the Scott Act as applicable to counties, and we looked around to see what would be the easiest method of getting an expression of opinion that would be entitled to respect as representing the volume of opinion in a province. It seemed to us that the legislature, after all, is a body of men selected by the people from all over the province, and in this regard, and as a rule, I think you can take the majority of the legislature as being representative of public opinion in the country. It does happen, however, that public opinion changes; that the members of the legislature perhaps do not change quite as quickly, and that public opinion gets a little ahead or perhaps sometimes falls a little behind, and you may have a moment at which the majority of any parliament or any legislature does not actually represent the people. On the other hand, prohibition after all is not a thing that is vital this year and ceases to be vital next, it is a measure which must be in effect for a considerable time after it comes into force. It may be annoying to the people of a province to find after they do desire this plebiscite that they have elected members who will not carry out their will, but it will only delay the matter for a short time.

I oppose the plebiscite altogether and therefore am not going to argue it; but if you only want machinery to start the plebiscite why not take the Governor in Council of the province? There is a body that is constantly meeting, and all they have to do is simply to grant the plebiscite if desired. Surely the government of a province is big enough for that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think there is a widespread impression in the country that this Bill is in the nature of prohibition throughout the Dominion. If I understand the minister aright, and read the Act aright, it has nothing to do with Dominion prohibi-

tion. Neither has it really anything to do with provincial prohibition otherwise than being in the nature of an enabling measure which permits the provinces to take a plebiscite under certain circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It does not permit the
provinces to take a plebiscite?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I mean it permits the Dominion to take a plebiscite for a province at the request of that province, It is not a measure of Dominion prohibition and not a provincial prohibition measure. As a prohibition measure therefore it is humbug. In other words. . .
What would my hon. friend have?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend's doctrine apparently is that all things in this world are divided into three classes-Dominion things, provincial things, and humbug. He says this is not a Dominion measure, and because, in his opinion, it is provincial it is necessarily humbug.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: As a prohibition measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, as a provincial
measure. The hon. gentleman's proposition is that a provincial measure, conditional for its effect upon the will of the people, is necessarily humbug as a prohibition measure. This is a Dominion-wide measure of conditional prohibition and it is for the people of every section to have it if they want to have it. The principle of this measure is the recognition of the right of the people to have their own will carried out, and that is what my hon. friend describes as ''humbug".

I would like to call the attention of the minister to section 152 which is under consideration, providing that upon receipt of a resolution the Governor in Council shall issue a proclamation for a vote. Is not that contradictory? And should not that be read subject to subsection 2 of section 156?
