Mr. LAFORTUNE (Jacques - Cartier). (Translation) :	Mr. Chairman, a very
active campaign has been carried on, in the several provinces of the Dominion, during many years; against intemperance; associations of every description, organizations of every nature, the municipal authorities and the clergy are leagued against the traffic in intoxicating liquors, and I am myself a member of those associations. I am a temperate man, having never made use of liquor or tobacco.
Hear, hear.

I have lived up to this time without making use of either, and my health has been all the better for it. Why talk of a referendum, Mr. Chairman? Is not public opinion sufficiently known? Has not this temperance question been fully discussed by the people of the different provinces, and is it not a fact that prohibitive measures have been enacted by all the legislatures? Why should we seek a further expression of public opinion? Why should we burden the country with another heavy expenditure when it is admitted that our financeis are in such a woeful condition? I am satisfied that the people's opinion on this question could never be better known than it is at present, and I claim that an appeal to the people is by no means necessary under the circumstances.
I shall refer, for instance, to the beautiful province of Ontario which recently started a great agitation in order to secure the complete elimination of alcoholic beverages. The western provinces, the Maritime provinces and the province of Quebec have also moved in that same direction. Yes, Mr. Chairman, fabulous sums were expended towards restricting th*>
manufacture and sale of intoxicating liquors. Such being the facts, would it not be foolish, now, to say that, if the provinces are not satisfied, a plebiscite will be demanded and the people called upon to render their verdict or, in other words, that we shall spend thousands of dollars to learn what we alreaday know, nay, what we have known for a long time, namely: that the liquor traffic is the most pernicious source of all the crime? which are perpetrated? No, you will never succeed in making the people more sober as long as the manufacture and the import

ation of alcoholic beverages are left untrammelled. A province may happen to pass a regulation, a law .prohibit the sale of intoxicating liquors, but the adjoining province may abstain from doing so. Hence, the drunkards, being unable to secure on the spot what they want, will go and get it in that adjoining province, and so, drunkenness and intemperance will persist, and our penitentiaries and jails will continue getting a full quota of criminal, and our .asylums, their full quota of destitute. Such is the result of the manufacture and sale of spirits in the country. May .1 add that, if we were to admit the principle set forth in the Bill now submitted to the House, we would be undoing heretofore the work accomplished by the several temperance organizations in every province of the Dominion, and that work would have to be taken up once more, as though nothing had ever been done. Mr. Chairman, I repeat that if spirits can be manufactured and imported from one province into another, they will continue to flow as they did in the past, we shall see them in quantities in the cellars of those who pose as being apostles of temperance though addicted, to drinking. While the blessings of temperance are being preached, heaps of barrels, cases and jugs will be seen everywhere. The use of intoxicating liquors results in destroying the force and vitality of the race, and it is our duty to fight that pest in every possible way.

(Text): Order. We are discussing section 152 of the Bill and rule 13 prescribe that speeches in Committee of the Whole must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
Mr. LAFORTUNE. (Translation): I do not quite understand. If Mr. Chairman would kindly repeat that remark in the language which I speak, it would be easier for me to catch the meaning of it.
'(Text). Would you be kind enough, Mr. Chairman, to repeat what you have just stated? I may then probably be in a better position to see whether I am .right or wrong. I do not want to discuss your ruling, Sir.

My ruling was that as the clause of the Bill now before the committee is number 152, the hon. member should confine his remarks to that clause, inasmuch as rule 13 says that speeches in Committee of the Whole must he strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
The whole Bill is found in section 1.
That is what I understand, Mr. Chairman.
So long as the hon. member's remarks are strictly relevant to the clause under consideration he is quite in order.
"Carried," "carried."

I realize, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. gentlemen who say: Carried, carried, may have their cellars replete with all their requirements, .and as a rule, this class of people are such .as are the most enthousiastic temperance supporters in the country. They are prone to meddle with other people's business, but they draw the line at their own shortcomings.
Our hospitals are taxed to their capacity with patients, unhappy victims of conditions resulting from intemperance and who a,re now depending upon the State for their care and treatment. The .great majority of public inmates in our asylums for the insane are men or women whose health and minds have been wrecked through the same evil which is also responsible for numberless oases of dire want and hardships of all kinds.
In the constituency which it is my privilege to represent, a by-law was passed by the .municipality prohibiting the sale of liquor, and although this was followed by strong action in order to have the by-law repealed, the majority of voters decided that the new order of things was to endure and as a result, local option was continued.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I have had many poor mothers approach me who begged for my support, saying:	Pray, dear sir, when
before Parliament, insist upon the passing of a law of prohibition for the country as a whole. Since my husband has no longer the opportunity of patronizing the corner saloon, how things have changed! Myself and my children a;re 'beltter cared for; every day of the week is a working day for their father, whereas formerly he ill treated me - and all his wages were spent on liquor. Now he hands me his wages every Saturdy evening, and instead of
f
staying out at night drinking and playing cards until four or five in the morning, he comes bade home early, takes a good night's rest, and we are happy.
Mr. Speaker and hon gentlemen, who now are paying such a religious respectful attention to my words, you are not without being aware as well as myself, if not better, that this is a fact, and you appreciate that this is a common happening at the present time throughout the land.
But no sooner does the thought of carrying out any reforms or doing away with a bad habit, occur to their mind than people are seized with a dread of the strong arm of trade, they are afraid that the manufacturers, importers, distillers of intoxicating liquors, powerful and wealthy men as they are, having their say in an election, may turn round and oppose this Government. So they say: Let us hold with the hare and run with the hounds; let us assume no responsibility.
I venture to say this to the hon. minister, who is now following my address (Sir George Foster). Do not act the coward; take the initiative and bring down a Bill providing for total prohibition, so as to relieve the situation; but you shrink back, because you will not take the responsibility before the electors of this country.
A few moments ago, the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) was put in a similar predicament to that I find myself in. His feelings were somewhat hurt by the remarks made by the hon. leader of the Opposition. I sincerely say that I have much respect for the hon. Minister of Justice, but let me tell him, voicing as I do the sentiment of my electors, that he is not in earnest about this measure .being passed into law. He wants to temporize, he wants to relieve himself of responsibility. My hon. friend said to himself: Let us keep watch over the situation and we shall abide by the decision taken by the provinces; we shall bring the matter up again, and when a general election is held we shall perhaps 'be absolved by the .people.
Well, Mr. Chairman, there are in my district 'very important concerns, which manufacture intoxicating liquors, there are influential distillers, but I intend to say to them, in due time: "My duty first, last and always." If you are able to do away with me as a representative of the people, very well; but I shall have discharged my duty at any rate; I shall have no qualms of conscience over the efforts I have put forth to reform bad habits, to make my electors more temperate and more thrifty,

but I do not disclaim responsibility for the stand I take here, as a representative of the people. In the meantime, I say this to the hon. minister: The Bill that you brought down some time ago, does not tally with the request, coming from the people of the Western provinces, from the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. All the provinces in this Dominion of ours advocate the passage of a law -for total prohibition by Parliament. It 's the trend of public opinion. Protestant ministers of every denomination have never relaxed their efforts and the Roman Catholic clergy likewise have bent all their endeavours towards the bringing about of the conditions now prevailing; under their leadership, the cause of temperance has made very substantial progress. They trusted that this Government, at the present session or at the next one, as soon as an opportunity offered for expressing their views, would have taken a decided stand and passed an Act providing for prohibition.
When those clergymen learn by the press, on Monday morning, that the provinces still enjoy their rights of option between prohibition and the traffic in intoxicating beverages, they will be grieved sorrily, and I venture to say that you are far from coming up to the expectations entertained by clergymen of the two largest religious denominations in this country.
Carried.
Order.

In regard to that
temperance issue, there is practically a consensus of opinion in this fair Canada of ours; however, I admit that perhaps there are pros and cons. Many people say that it is not -so great an evil to allow farmers, labourers and everybody else to take a little drop before meals. Many people maintain also that we should try to spread temperance by moral -suasion, good order and example, that it would be easy toy those means to check this liquor evil and to promote temperance which makes for the happiness of the people. But I do" not subscribe to that opinion, Mr. Chairman.
For over fifty years, this' temperance question has -been discussed under all its different aspects before large public gatherings, and yet we have made very little progress. Why? Because of this old saying: "Habit is second nature," and the man who has been addicted for years to intemperance, finds it very hard to break a settled habit,
I am prepared to admit that a few people

-could be reclaimed, but it would -be a small minority indeed, whereas if the members of this Administration were willing to cooperate and help in solving this liquor problem, we should get far better results
Mr. Chairman, it is stated that if the Government puts a stop to manufacturing and selling intoxicating liquors, they would be- deprived of a large amount of revenue, that there would be a falling off in the duties collected, if we are prevented from importing alcoholic liquors into Canada. With all due respect I -answer: No. I assert that the sums that are annually spent by the Government for the maintenance of the judiciary and the criminal -machinery -and for the upkeep "of prisoners in jails throughout the country, exceed -considerably the revenue derived from that branch of trade.
I say that prohibition would result in abating to a great extent the number of criminals, of patients in the hospitals, of destitutes kept in the poorhouses and in the workhouses at the expense of the State and that, far from being the loser, the State would realize, thereby, a substantial benefit. Mr. Chairman, we must not forget to take into consideration the -many joys which we sh-all have brought to the homes of our people if we succeed in checking this evil, and the happiness of the whole population would then mean ample and more than ample compensation for the lost, of revenue entailed, a revenue which was derived from that line of trade. Under the circumstances, why should we hesitate any longer? I consider, Mr. -Chairman, that this question is most important for the electors whom I have the honour to represent, and I should consider that I was recreant to my duty if I failed to do my utmost to prevent the enactment of this measure which, far from promoting the cause of temperance, rather t-end3 to encourage the use of intoxicating liquors.

To me, this is not a question of pleasure; it is a question of duty. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is not very generous; I have never interfered when he has taken up three or four hours in making a speech to the House. I feel it my duty to do the best I can to convince hon. members that they are wrong; that is my only desire.
(translation): What have we seen, Mr. Chairman, since mitigated prohibition was imposed in the several provinces? A great number of stills were seized which had been hidden in cellars, or in barns, in the woods or in the fields, and by means of which intoxicating liquors were made, with the result that the provincial laws forbidding this manufacture were eluded and frustrated.
What have we seen in the province of Ontario as well as in the other provinces, not excepting Quebec? We have seen a great number of .seizures made by the ' revenue officers, who also found large quantities of intoxicating liquors in cellars, in underground recesses, in the fields and in the woods. Those liquors, manufactured underhand, are not alcohol, they are real poisons.	.
And this is tolerated by the Government. When things have gone so far as to make it necessary for them to do away with such conditions, they talk about a referendum, and the advisability of consulting the people. We shall see, then, do they say, what people's opinion is, .as though we were unaware of .the fact that thi.s opinion
i.s well moulded into shape and was put on record whenever an opportunity offered for the people making its voice heard.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I claim that this Government is unwilling to face the situation .and instead of introducing la prohibition Bill it brings down a half-measure which will not be satisfactory to the electors of the .Dominion.
*Several of the hon. ministers and members would like me to take my seat forthwith, so. that this half-measure .might be allowed to pass. Well, I must tell them that in spite of all the work which they may have done in behalf of temperance, they are not serious when they pretend to be temperance men.
Great work was achieved by associations of ladies who held meeting, travelling all over the country, in their endeavour to have temperance laws enacted in order to uplift public morality; but those ladies will find that they are not given a fair deal when the Government denies them its help, when they are losing the fruits of their labour, of the efforts, which they put forth during more than ten years and when the result of their activities is reduced to nothing
You are in favour of this Bill?

No, no, I am obsolutely opposed to the Bill which is now before ns, because it does not go . far enough, because it leaves the people free to drink as they used to in the past. The Canadian people want no such legislation.
I shall now follow the advice of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster). I was bound to register any protest against this Bill, and I think I have done so in such a manner .as to warrant my electors in giving me credit for my efforts in that direction. Those will be my concluding remarks. I shall now resume my seat, thanking, at the same time the hon. gentlemen for having so intently listened to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is an Act to provide for those who brought prohibition into force, because in their judgment it was desirable, the very reasonable right of putting an end to the operation of a law, which operation rested upon the expression of their will.
That may be done on the same class of vote as that which brought prohibition into force?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Section agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I beg to move that the Bill be further amended by adding as sec-

tion 2 of the Bill, subsection 1, the following:
2.	(1) When any Intoxicating: liquor is seized and brought before any judge of the sessions of the peace, recorder, police magistrate, stipendiary magistrate, two justices of the peace or any magistrate having the power or authority of two or more justices of the peace, in pursuance of the provisions of this Act, and the consignor or consignee or owner thereof or person entitled thereto or claiming the same cannot be ascertained, and if no person establishes a claim to the possession of such intoxicating liquor within a period of fifteen days after the seizure thereof as aforesaid, or within such extended time as the judge of the sessions of the peace, recorder, police magistrate, stipendiary magistrate, two justices of the peace or magistrate having the power or authority of two or more justices of the peace, may allow, or as may otherwise be allowed by any competent tribunal, then the judge of the sessions of the peace, recorder, police magistrate, stipendiary magistrate, two justices of the peace or magistrate having the power or authority of two or more justices of the peace who issued the warrant in execution of which such intoxicating liquor was seized, or, in the case of the death, absence or inability to act of such judge of the sessions of the peace recorder, police magistrate, stipendiary magistrate, two justices of the peace or magistrate having the power or authority of two or more justices of the peace, any other judge of the sessions of the peace, recorder, police magistrate, stipendiary magistrate, two justices of the peace or magistrate having the power or authority of two or more justices of the peace, may adjudge and declare such intoxicating liquor, together wfith all kegs, barrels, cases, boxes, bottles, packages, containers and other receptacles of any kind whatever found containing the same to be forfeited to the Crown.
This is precisely the same provision in regard to the disposition of liquor seized and for which an owner cannot be found that we made this afternoon in connection with Bill No. 27.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Subsection agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Subsection 2 is likewise a reproduction of the clause adopted this afternoon. It is as follows:
(2) As soon as any intoxicating Lquor and the receptacles containing the same are forfeited to the Crown, the judge of the sessions of the peace, recorder, police magistrate, stipendiary magistrate, two justices of the peace or magistrate having the power or authority of two or more justices of the peace by whom [DOT]such forfeiture is adjudged and declared shall immediately transmit to the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue a notice in writing specifying the quantities and descriptions of the intoxicating liquor so forfeited, and shall over that such intoxicating, liquor shall immediately be deposited in a Custom Bonding Warehouse within the province wherein such intoxicating liquor is forfeited as aforesaid, to be disposed of as the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue may direct.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Subsection agreed to.
Bill as amended reported.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: When shall the Bill be read a third time?
On Monday.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The Bill, of course, can only be read a third time by unanimous consent at this sitting.
Motion for third reading agreed to and Bill read the third time and passed.
On the motion of Sir George Foster for the adjournment of the House:

Has any time been
fixed for Prorogation or is there any' business left for another sitting?

The only business that is left for the Commons is the Supply Bill which we will take up immediately the House assembles at eleven o'clock on Monday. Then there may be some business that will come to us from the Senate, but if the Upper House makes as good progress on Monday morning as we have made to-night-

Sunday
morning.

-and in the small portion of Sunday that we have used up in a good cause, I think we shall be able to prorogue about four o'clock in the afternoon.
Motion agreed to and House adjourned at 12.48 a.m. (Sunday).
Monday, ,November 10, 1919.
